Utopian Socialists: Owen, Fourier, Saint-Simon
Socialism before Marx

Marx did not invent socialism. By 1840 it was already a lively set of experiments and sermons. Marx and Engels called their predecessors utopian and their own method scientific . To judge that claim, you need to know who they were arguing with. The question these early thinkers asked is still live: if industry makes some people rich and many people miserable, can we fix it by persuasion and example, or only by struggle?
Factories, revolution and misery

Two shocks made the field. The French Revolution (1789) promised equality but left property untouched. The Industrial Revolution created mills, slums, child labour and cycles of slump. Cities like Manchester grew faster than their drains. The word "socialism" spread in the 1820s-30s, in Britain among Owen's followers and in France among Saint-Simon's. At first it meant social organisation of production, in contrast to cut-throat individualism. It did not yet mean a party or a revolution.
Robert Owen: change the environment

Robert Owen (1771-1858), a Welsh mill-owner, ran New Lanark in Scotland from 1800. He cut hours, banned child work for the youngest, built schools and shops, and still made profit. In A New View of Society (1813) he argued that character is formed by circumstances, so better surroundings make better people. Owen later funded the cooperative colony of New Harmony, Indiana (1825). It broke up within about three years amid quarrels. He then helped found early trade unions and cooperatives, and the Grand National Consolidated Trades Union (1834) collapsed quickly.
Fourier: attractions and phalansteries

Charles Fourier (1772-1837) wrote Theory of the Four Movements (1808). He held that civilisation frustrates human passions, and that work could be made attractive. He proposed self-sufficient communities, phalansteries of about 1,600 people, where tasks are rotated by taste. He was an early critic of the way marriage kept women dependent; the word "feminism" is often credited to him. Some of his claims were fantastic, such as seas turning to lemonade. Marx and Engels still praised his sharp critique of bourgeois society.
Saint-Simon: rule by the productive

Henri de Saint-Simon (1760-1825) argued in L'Industrie (1816-18) and Le Nouveau Christianisme (1825) that society should be run by industrialists, scientists and workers (the industriels ) rather than idle nobles and landlords. He wanted administration of things, not rule over people, and care for "the most numerous and poorest class". His followers split into a technocratic wing, which influenced French engineers and bankers, and a quasi-religious cult. Engels later borrowed the phrase "administration of things" from this tradition.
Why Marx called them utopian

In the Communist Manifesto (1848) Marx and Engels say the utopians saw the class antagonism but not the proletariat's historical role. They appealed to all of society, even the rich, and rejected political action. Engels' Socialism: Utopian and Scientific (1880) added that these thinkers lacked a theory of how capitalism works and changes. The fair counterpoint: the utopians were not naive about power. Owen met ministers and kings. Fourier waited for a patron daily at noon. But they lacked a plan for taking power.
Communes that failed, ideas that stayed

Owenite and Fourierist communities in the US (New Harmony, Brook Farm, over 20 Fourierist "phalanxes" in the 1840s) mostly lasted only a few years. Typical causes: weak capital, quarrels, outsiders who did not share the faith. Yet cooperatives survived. The Rochdale Pioneers (1844) set up a shop that became the template for the consumer co-op movement. Factory reform, free schools and labour unions all drew on this tradition.
Marxist and liberal objections

Marx and Engels: moral appeals do not change a system that rewards exploitation. Islands of cooperation get crushed or absorbed by the market. Liberals: Hayek and Popper saw in Saint-Simon's technocrats and Fourier's regimented harmony an early blueprint for planning from above. Popper called this "utopian social engineering". Anarchists: Proudhon and others valued the voluntary, local element but felt Marx used "utopian" as a cheap way to dismiss it. Historical record: Saint-Simon's cult, Owen's quarrels and Fourier's fantasies show that good intentions are not a theory of institutions.
Cooperatives, ashrams and planning

The cooperative idea reached India with the Co-operative Credit Societies Act (1904) and later the dairy cooperatives behind Amul (1946, Verghese Kurien). Gandhi's ashrams and Vinoba Bhave's Bhoodan (1951) were village-level experiments in sharing that resemble the utopian mood more than Marx. Robert Owen's influence is visible in the Gandhian trusteeship idea: owners hold wealth as trustees for society. Marxists such as E.M.S. Namboodiripad criticised it as moral persuasion without class struggle.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Utopian socialists criticised industrial capitalism before Marx. Owen stressed environment; Fourier passion and work; Saint-Simon industrial planning. Marx called them utopian for lacking a theory of class struggle and of political power. Their communes mostly failed; their cooperatives and reforms endured. Critics see both naivety and a seed of top-down planning. Debate questions Is persuasion by example ever enough to change an economic system? Did Marx treat the utopians fairly?
Hegel, the Young Hegelians and Feuerbach
The philosophy behind Marx

Marx's first teachers were philosophers, not economists. If you do not see how he turned Hegel "right side up", phrases like dialectic, alienation and historical materialism sound like jargon. The issue: does history move because of ideas or because of material life? The whole Marxist tradition rests on that choice.
Germany in the 1830s-40s

Germany was a patchwork of states, with censorship and little industry. Philosophy became the place where politics was debated. After Hegel died in 1831 his followers split. The "Old Hegelians" defended the Prussian state. The Young Hegelians in Berlin used his method against religion and monarchy. Marx studied law, then philosophy, and took a doctorate on Democritus and Epicurus (1841). He joined the Rheinische Zeitung in Cologne in 1842, where he met real social questions like wood-theft laws.
Hegel: spirit and the dialectic

G.W.F. Hegel (1770-1831) saw history as the unfolding of reason or Spirit ( Geist ), moving through contradictions: an idea meets its opposite and both are lifted into a higher unity. The Phenomenology of Spirit (1807) and Philosophy of Right (1821) apply this to mind and to the state. Freedom grows as history advances. The popular triad "thesis, antithesis, synthesis" is not Hegel's own phrase; it is a later shorthand. Marx kept the idea that change comes from internal conflict, not from outside pushes.
The Young Hegelians and the critique of religion

Bruno Bauer, David Strauss ( Life of Jesus , 1835) and others turned the dialectic against Christianity and the state. For them, criticising religion was the first step to freedom. Marx gradually concluded that this was too abstract: attacking ideas leaves the conditions that produce them untouched. In 1843 he wrote that "the criticism of religion" must become the criticism of earth, law and politics.
Feuerbach: man makes God

Ludwig Feuerbach in The Essence of Christianity (1841) argued that God is human nature projected outward. People pour their best qualities into an imaginary being and then bow to it. Marx accepted this "alienation" idea but, in the Theses on Feuerbach (1845), said Feuerbach stayed contemplative. Thesis 11 is famous: philosophers have only interpreted the world; the point is to change it. Marx insisted that religion itself comes from a world that needs consoling.
Turning Hegel on his feet

In the afterword to Capital (1873) Marx said the dialectic stood on its head in Hegel and must be set on its feet. Ideas are not the engine; material life, labour and class relations are. Materialism replaced Spirit; dialectic (conflict inside systems) survived. The German Ideology (1845-46, with Engels) mocked the Young Hegelians for fighting "phrases" with phrases. It was not published in their lifetimes.
From seminar to politics

Marx's path shows the move. The Prussian state shut his paper in 1843. He moved to Paris, met workers and Engels, and wrote the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts (1844). Philosophy now pointed to a social class, the proletariat, as the agent that could abolish both religion's consolations and the conditions behind them. Hegel's legacy split: the right defended the state; the left became Marx's revolution.
Was the inversion coherent?

Liberals (Popper, The Open Society , 1945) argue that Hegel's historicism justifies authority: if history has a direction, those who claim to know it may override individuals. Analytical Marxists (G.A. Cohen) say the dialectic adds mystery, and that Marx's real arguments can be stated in plain logic. Feuerbach and humanists thought Marx dropped the human being for abstract classes. Historians note that the "turn to materialism" came in a few months of 1844-45 and was never fully argued by Marx himself; Engels filled in later.
Hegel in Indian thought

Hegel wrote disparagingly of India in his Lectures on the Philosophy of History , treating it as a stage that history had passed. Indian thinkers answered in different ways. M.N. Roy and early communists took Marxism as the modern science; Radhakrishnan read Hegel against Vedanta; later scholars such as D.D. Kosambi used materialist method on ancient India without Hegelian metaphysics. Postcolonial critics (Ranajit Guha, Dipesh Chakrabarty) argue that Hegelian stage-theories write India out of history.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Marx started as a Young Hegelian, a left reader of Hegel. The dialectic: change arises from internal contradiction. Feuerbach showed religion as human projection; Marx said people must change the conditions that produce it. Marx put the dialectic on its feet: material life drives history. Critics say historicism can excuse authority. Debate questions Is Marx more indebted to Hegel than he admitted? Can ideas change society without a change in material conditions?
Proudhon, Blanqui and the Early Workers' Movements
Three rival roads

Before 1848 the workers' movement had three tendencies: mutual aid and anti-statism (Proudhon), conspiratorial insurrection (Blanqui), and the democratic, mass-organising Chartists. Marx fought and borrowed from all three. Their arguments about reform, revolution and the party come back through the rest of this course.
Workers organise

After 1815, craftsmen and mill workers formed mutual societies, secret clubs and unions, often illegal. Combination laws in Britain were repealed in 1824. The Lyon silk-weavers ( canuts ) rose in 1831 and 1834. In Britain, the People's Charter (1838) demanded votes for all men, secret ballot and pay for MPs. In Europe, 1848 was the year of revolutions.
Proudhon: property is theft

Pierre-Joseph Proudhon (1809-65), a printer from Besançon, wrote What Is Property? (1840): "property is theft", meaning unearned income from ownership. He wanted free credit through a People's Bank, mutual exchange among small producers and federation instead of state power. In System of Economic Contradictions (1846) he claimed to show the philosophy of poverty. He called himself an anarchist, the first to do so positively.
Marx versus Proudhon

Marx answered with The Poverty of Philosophy (1847), a pun on Proudhon's subtitle. He charged that Proudhon wanted to keep commodity production and money while removing their effects, and that categories like "justice" ignored history. Yet Proudhon's federal, small-scale ideas lived on in the First International and in the Paris Commune (1871).
Blanqui: the revolutionary minority

Louis Auguste Blanqui (1805-81) spent roughly half his adult life in prison. He believed a small, disciplined secret society could seize power in Paris and rule temporarily on behalf of the people (a "dictatorship"). Blanqui's tactics stressed conspiracy, not mass organisation. Lenin later admired his determination while insisting on a party rooted in the working class.
Chartists, Louis Blanc and the national workshops

Chartists mixed petitions, strikes and mass meetings. Their 1839, 1842 and 1848 petitions all failed in Parliament. Louis Blanc ( The Organisation of Labour , 1839) proposed state-backed workshops and the slogan "from each according to his abilities, to each according to his needs." In 1848 the Paris national workshops, a pale version of his plan, closed in June; the workers' rising was crushed by General Cavaignac with several thousand killed.
1848 and its lesson

The Manifesto (written for the Communist League, published February 1848) met a continent in revolt. The upheavals produced republics, then reaction. Marx concluded that workers must organise independently of middle-class liberals and that state power was the central prize. Engels later said barricade tactics were obsolete as armies modernised. The First International (1864), with Marx as leading organiser, brought Proudhonists, trade unionists and Blanquists into one body, until it split in 1872.
What the early movements got wrong, or right

Marx on Proudhon: a petty-bourgeois dreamer. Anarchists: Marx's centralism threatened freedom, a charge Bakunin pressed. Liberals: Blanqui's minority rule shows the authoritarian risk of "revolution on behalf of the people". Historians: Proudhon was no feminist: he defended patriarchal family hierarchy and held racist and antisemitic views, a stain on his legacy. Chartism failed to win its six points by 1848, though almost all but annual parliaments were enacted later.
Mutualism, insurrection and early labour

Early Indian labour organising echoed these arguments: Narayan Meghaji Lokhande set up the Bombay Millhands' Association (1890); N.M. Joshi and the AITUC (1920) followed the British trade-union model. M.N. Roy's generation read Blanquist-style insurrection in the Kanpur and Meerut conspiracy cases (1924, 1929). The Gandhian cooperative-and-village idea has Proudhonian overtones of small producers, mutual aid and decentralisation, though Gandhi never read him closely.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Proudhon: property is theft, mutual exchange and federation. Blanqui: insurrection by a disciplined minority. Chartists and Louis Blanc: mass pressure and state-backed labour. 1848 taught Marx that workers must act as an independent class. Anarchist and liberal critics saw authoritarian risks in both centralism and conspiracy. Debate questions Is a small disciplined minority ever a legitimate vehicle for revolution? Would a Proudhon-style economy of small producers work in a modern industrial society?
Historical Materialism
A theory of why history moves

Historical materialism is the core of Marx's thought: the claim that how people produce their living shapes their laws, politics and ideas. Believe it and the French Revolution, the British empire and the fall of Rome all look different. Reject it and you ask why so many historians still use parts of it.
Marx in his study

The classic statement is a short passage in the Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy (1859). Earlier, The German Ideology (1845-46, with Engels) argued that "life is not determined by consciousness, but consciousness by life". Marx wrote little more on method; the term "historical materialism" is Engels's.
Forces and relations of production

Forces of production are tools, machines, skills, knowledge and raw materials. Relations of production are the social arrangements of ownership and control: lord and serf, master and slave, capitalist and wage-worker. Together they form the mode of production . Examples: ancient slavery, feudalism, capitalism.
Base and superstructure

In the 1859 Preface Marx says the economic structure is the "real foundation" on which a legal and political superstructure rises, with matching forms of consciousness. Law, religion, art and the state are not independent; they reflect and protect the dominant economic interests. The metaphor is a building. Engels later wrote (letter to Bloch, 1890) that the economy is determining only "in the last instance", and that politics and ideas react back on it.
Contradiction and revolution

At a certain stage, the forces of production grow beyond the relations that contain them. Feudal guilds block factories; capitalist ownership blocks planned use of technology. The relations then become "fetters", and an era of social revolution begins. Marx offers a sequence: primitive communism, ancient, feudal, capitalist, then communism, though he warned in letters (1877, to a Russian journal) against treating this as a universal template.
Class struggle as the engine

The Communist Manifesto (1848) opens: the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles. Freeman and slave, lord and serf, guild-master and journeyman stood in constant opposition. Capitalism simplifies the picture into two great camps, bourgeoisie and proletariat. Class, for Marx, is defined by one's relation to the means of production, not income or status.
Historians who used it

Marxist history made a mark: E.P. Thompson's The Making of the English Working Class (1963), Christopher Hill on the English Revolution, Eric Hobsbawm's Age of Revolution (1962), and the Annales school's interest in material life. The "Brenner debate" (1976-) argued over whether feudalism fell from trade or from class struggle in the countryside. In the Soviet Union the theory hardened into a five-stage dogma taught as compulsory truth, and used to justify decisions as "historically necessary".
Challenges to the theory

Popper ( The Poverty of Historicism , 1957): claims of laws of history are unfalsifiable. Weber ( The Protestant Ethic , 1905): ideas such as Protestant discipline also shape economies. G.A. Cohen ( Karl Marx's Theory of History , 1978) defends a technological reading but admits it needs a functional explanation. Non-Marxist and Marxist critics point out that revolutions happened first in peasant Russia and China, not mature capitalist societies. Anarchists doubt that the state is merely superstructure; Eurocentrism is a charge against the stage sequence.
The Asiatic mode and Indian history

Marx wrote on India in the New York Daily Tribune (1853), calling British rule destructive and regenerating, and discussing an "Asiatic mode" with village communities and a state owning the land. This is contested. D.D. Kosambi (1956), R.S. Sharma ( Indian Feudalism , 1965) and Irfan Habib ( Agrarian System of Mughal India , 1963) applied Marxist method; critics such as Romila Thapar broadly accept the method but dispute rigid feudalism models, and others say caste cannot be reduced to class.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Social life rests on the mode of production: forces plus relations. The economic base conditions law, politics and ideas. Revolution comes when relations fetter productive forces. Class struggle moves history; class is relation to means of production. Critics attack determinism, the stage sequence and Eurocentrism. Debate questions Does material interest explain religion and nationalism well enough? Was the Soviet five-stage scheme faithful to Marx or a distortion?
Alienation and Human Nature
Why work can feel empty

Long before the Soviet Union, Marx asked a human question: why do people who make things feel least at home in the world they make? His 1844 notebooks on alienation are now the favourite starting point for humanist Marxists, and remain a lively challenge to modern work.
Paris, 1844

The Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 were written when Marx, aged 26, was reading political economy for the first time. They were not published until 1932, which changed how Marxism was read. They combine Hegel, Feuerbach and Adam Smith in an argument about labour.
Four kinds of alienation

Under capitalism, the worker is estranged in four ways: - From the product : it belongs to someone else, and the more produced, the poorer the worker. - From the activity : work is forced, not creative. - From species-being : human beings are distinctively creative and social, yet work reduces them to survival. - From other people : others become competitors or tools.
Human nature as free, conscious labour

Marx rejects fixed human nature. In the Sixth Thesis on Feuerbach he writes that essence is "the ensemble of the social relations". But he also uses the idea of species-being : humans make things consciously, "according to the laws of beauty", and so realise themselves in production. Estranged labour reduces the free activity to a means of survival.
Commodity fetishism

In Capital (1867), chapter 1, Marx extends the theme. Relations between people appear as relations between things: shoes trade for hats at certain prices, and the social labour behind them vanishes. We bow to market "laws" as earlier people bowed to gods. This is the mature version of alienation: a power made by people controls them.
The overcoming of alienation

Marx's future society is not simply equal distribution. It is one where work becomes self-expression and society consciously controls production. The German Ideology imagines a world where one can "hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon, rear cattle in the evening, criticise after dinner". The picture is deliberately playful, and a standing joke for critics.
Alienation and the factory

Worker complaints about the assembly line gave the idea a concrete form: Taylorism, Henry Ford's line (1913), call-centre scripts, gig platforms. Studies by Robert Blauner ( Alienation and Freedom , 1964) found that alienation varies with technology. State socialist factories did not escape; Soviet and Chinese workers also met quotas, supervisors and shortages.
Early Marx versus late Marx

Althusser ( For Marx , 1965) argued there is an "epistemological break": the humanist 1844 Marx was pre-scientific and ideological. Humanists (Fromm, Marcuse, Kolakowski) said the break is a myth and that morality is central. Liberals and Hayek say freedom needs markets, and that "true" self-realisation is easily used to override actual wishes. Feminists note that the focus on wage work ignores unpaid labour.
Alienation and Indian thinkers

Gandhi's critique of machine civilisation in Hind Swaraj (1909) and his stress on bodily labour is an independent protest against alienated work. The Indian humanist Marxist tradition, including M.N. Roy's "Radical Humanism" (1940s), took up the 1844 themes. In politics, bonded labour and caste-based work show that estrangement is also about unfreedom: Ambedkar noted that caste is a division of labourers, not of labour.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways The 1844 Manuscripts describe four kinds of alienation under capitalism. Human nature is social, creative labour, not a fixed essence. Commodity fetishism extends the theme in Capital (1867). Communism means conscious control of production and meaningful work. Critics dispute whether early Marx is the true Marx and whether the ideal is workable. Debate questions Is alienation a useful way of understanding modern gig work? Can a theory of human fulfilment be pursued without coercion?
Capital: Value, Surplus Value and Crisis
Marx's economics in plain words

Capital (Volume 1, 1867) is the book most people cite and few read. Its question is simple: if markets exchange equal values, where does profit come from? Marx's answer, surplus value , is the theoretical core of the claim that capitalism rests on exploitation.
From Smith and Ricardo to Marx

Marx built on the classical economists. Adam Smith ( Wealth of Nations , 1776) and David Ricardo (1817) held that the value of a good comes from labour. Marx wrote Volume 1 in London after years in the British Museum library. Engels edited Volumes 2 (1885) and 3 (1894) from Marx's notes after his death in 1883.
Value and the commodity

A commodity has use-value (usefulness) and exchange-value (what it trades for). Marx argues the value of commodities reflects the socially necessary labour time to produce them under average conditions. Money is the general form of value. Prices fluctuate, but over time they are ruled by labour content, he claims.
Surplus value and exploitation

The worker sells labour power , not labour. Its price, the wage, equals the cost of keeping the worker alive. But in a working day the worker produces more value than that. If a worker covers wages in 4 hours of a 10-hour day, the other 6 hours yield surplus value , taken by the capitalist. The rate of exploitation is surplus value divided by variable capital (wages). Exchange at the wage is fair on the surface; exploitation hides in the production process.
Accumulation and the falling rate of profit

Competition forces capitalists to invest in machines ( constant capital ). Since only living labour creates surplus value, Marx argues that a rising ratio of machines to labour tends to lower the rate of profit (Volume 3). Counter-forces exist: cheaper goods, longer hours, new markets. The industrial reserve army of unemployed keeps wages down. Capital concentrates into fewer, larger firms.
Crisis and the end of capitalism

Marx sees crises of overproduction and credit as built into the system: production expands faster than demand. Booms and slumps recur (1825, 1857, 1873...). In Volume 1 chapter 32 he predicts that "the expropriators are expropriated". He did not give a date, and in the Grundrisse (1857-58, published 1939-41) he even hints at automation reducing labour.
What the record shows

Real wages did rise in rich countries; Marx's "increasing misery" did not appear as a steady fall in living standards. But inequality fell in the mid-20th century, then rose again; Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2013) revived Marxian themes with data. Crises did recur: 1929, 2008. Concentration into giant firms is real. Yet capitalism proved adaptable through welfare states and credit.
Economists and Marxists

Böhm-Bawerk (1896) pointed to the "transformation problem": Marx's values and actual prices of production do not match neatly. Marginalists (Jevons, Menger, 1870s) say value comes from subjective utility, not labour. Okishio's theorem (1961) shows that cost-cutting innovation need not lower the profit rate. Joan Robinson thought the labour theory unnecessary; Analytical Marxists (Roemer) say exploitation can be defined without it. Hayek says prices carry information that labour times cannot.
Capital and Indian economics

Dadabhai Naoroji's drain theory ( Poverty and Un-British Rule in India , 1901) and R.C. Dutt's Economic History of India (1901-03) anticipate imperialism critiques. Post-Independence, P.C. Mahalanobis's Second Five-Year Plan (1956) drew on Soviet planning. Marxist economists such as Prabhat Patnaik and Utsa Patnaik ( Capital and Imperialism , 2021) continue the Marxian tradition; "Capital" was also the prop of arguments over agrarian classes (Mode of Production debate, 1970s).
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Value is socially necessary labour time; labour power is the commodity workers sell. Surplus value arises from unpaid surplus labour. Accumulation raises machinery and may lower the rate of profit. Crises are recurrent; Marx foresaw concentration and the "expropriation of the expropriators". The transformation problem and marginalism challenge the labour theory. Debate questions Does exploitation require the labour theory of value? Have welfare states disproved Marx's predictions or only postponed them?
Class, State and Revolution
Who rules, and how it ends

Marx has no single book on the state. Yet his scattered writings produced the most influential political claim of the 19th century: the state is a tool of the ruling class, and workers must seize it, then eventually abolish it. Everything from Lenin to the anarchist objection grows from this.
Class politics in three texts

Key texts: The Communist Manifesto (1848), The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte (1852) on the French coup of 1851, and The Civil War in France (1871). They show Marx moving from a simple model to subtler ones.
The state as committee of the bourgeoisie

The Manifesto says the executive of the modern state is "a committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie". Law protects property; police and army enforce it. Even universal suffrage may leave economic power untouched. Marx also said in a speech in Amsterdam (1872) that in Britain, the US and perhaps the Netherlands workers might win by peaceful means.
Relative autonomy: Bonapartism

In the Eighteenth Brumaire Marx shows Louis Napoleon ruling as the middle class gave up political power to protect its social position. The state, here, stands above classes in appearance, while serving the bourgeoisie's interest. Later Marxists use this to explain fascism and military regimes.
Class consciousness and the revolutionary agent

Marx distinguishes a class "in itself" (shared position) from a class "for itself" (aware and organised), in The Poverty of Philosophy (1847). Why the proletariat? It is numerous, concentrated in factories, has "nothing to lose but its chains", and its liberation requires abolishing class itself. Peasants, the "sack of potatoes" of the Brumaire, scatter and lack common organisation.
Revolution and the withering of the state

After revolution, workers use state power in a transitional period (the dictatorship of the proletariat, treated in the next lesson). As classes disappear, "the state is not abolished, it withers away", wrote Engels in Anti-Dühring (1878). Marx's Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875) sketches a lower and higher phase of communism, ending with "from each according to ability, to each according to needs".
What revolutions did

Every successful communist revolution (Russia 1917, China 1949, Cuba 1959) produced a stronger, not weaker, state. Party officials formed what Milovan Djilas called "the new class" (1957). Revolution came in peasant societies, often via war and a party, not from industrial workers alone. In wealthy democracies, electoral socialism (Sweden, Britain 1945) took the reform road Marx allowed.
State theory under fire

Anarchists (Bakunin, 1870s) predicted that a "workers' state" would become a new ruling class. Weber held the state is defined by monopoly of force, whatever the class. Pluralists (Dahl) show that democracies spread power among groups, not one class. Poulantzas and Miliband debated how far the state is controlled or structurally tied to capital in the 1970s. Liberals say that revolutionary violence rarely yields freedom. Historians observe that the working class shrank in many rich countries and splits by ethnicity, gender and sector.
Class or caste?

Indian Marxists argued over the agent. Ambedkar saw caste hierarchy as the primary oppression and wrote that a social revolution must precede an economic one; he worried that Marxism ignored the "graded inequality" of caste. The CPI under S.A. Dange pursued trade-union class politics; E.M.S. Namboodiripad later used class to explain Kerala's land reforms (1957 ministry, the first elected communist government in India). The Constitution's directive principles borrow some of the socialist language of the state as an agent of redistribution.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways The state, in Marx, serves the economic interests of the ruling class. Class consciousness is the shift from "in itself" to "for itself". Revolution is followed by a transitional state that is meant to wither away. Practice: communist states grew stronger and created new elites. Critics ask whether any state can wither, and whether class is the key axis. Debate questions Can democracy alone transform capitalism, as Marx's Amsterdam speech allowed? Is caste, gender or ethnicity a rival to class as the key line of conflict?
The Paris Commune and the Dictatorship of the Proletariat
Marx's only model, and a loaded phrase

Marx used the phrase "dictatorship of the proletariat" rarely. After the Paris Commune of 1871 he called the Commune its model. The phrase later justified Lenin and Stalin. The question is what he meant, and whether the Commune supports a democratic or an authoritarian reading.

France lost the Franco-Prussian War; Napoleon III fell in September 1870. Paris endured a siege. When the government of Thiers tried to seize the National Guard's cannon on 18 March 1871, Parisians rose. The Commune governed for 72 days (18 March to 28 May).
What the Commune did

Elected by universal male suffrage in Paris, it paid officials workers' wages, made them recallable, separated church and state, banned night work in bakeries, handed abandoned workshops to cooperatives and began free schooling. Women (Louise Michel, the Union des Femmes) played a major part. It was a federation of districts, not a seizure of the central state.
Marx: smash the state machine

In The Civil War in France (1871) Marx wrote that the working class "cannot simply lay hold of the ready-made state machinery". The Commune showed a different form: a working body, both executive and legislative, with recallable delegates. It was, he said, "the political form at last discovered" for economic emancipation. This is the text behind Lenin's State and Revolution (1917).
What "dictatorship" meant

Marx used the term in a letter to Weydemeyer (1852) and in the Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875): a "revolutionary dictatorship of the proletariat" in the transition between capitalism and communism. In the 19th century "dictatorship" recalled the Roman office: a temporary emergency rule. Engels in 1891 said: "Look at the Paris Commune. That was the Dictatorship of the Proletariat." The point: class rule, not one man's tyranny.
Repression and legacy

Government troops killed perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 in Bloody Week (estimates vary; some say more); tens of thousands were arrested or deported to New Caledonia. The Commune also executed hostages, including the Archbishop of Paris, and burned buildings, which critics stress. Lenin later asked whether the Bolsheviks would last longer than 72 days; in 1918 they passed that mark and danced in the snow, as the story goes. In Soviet usage, the phrase meant Party rule over every institution.
Democratic or authoritarian?

Kautsky ( The Dictatorship of the Proletariat , 1918) read Marx as meaning democratic majority rule and accused Lenin of betrayal. Lenin replied ( The Proletarian Revolution and the Renegade Kautsky , 1918) that it is class power based on force. Bakunin (1873) foresaw state bureaucrats. Liberals point out that the Commune lasted too briefly to prove anything and had tough measures (hostage-taking, closing newspapers). Historians (Robert Tombs) argue the Commune was more patriotic and republican than socialist. Luxemburg said "Freedom is always freedom for the one who thinks differently".
The Commune and the Indian left

Indian communists use the Commune as a symbol, with 18 March commemorations in left circles. The CPI(M) programme describes the party's aim as a "People's Democratic" state; it says that it works within the Constitution and the multi-party system, a position that sits between Kautsky and Lenin. Its governments in West Bengal (1977-2011, uninterrupted 34 years), Kerala and Tripura raise the question of whether a communist party can use bourgeois-democratic state power. Maoists in India reject this and call for armed overthrow.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways The Commune lasted 72 days (March to May 1871) and ended in massacre. Marx called it the political form for working-class emancipation: recallable officials on workers' wages. "Dictatorship of the proletariat" meant class rule during transition, but was read by Leninists as party rule. Kautsky and Luxemburg insisted on democracy; Lenin insisted on force. Historians debate how socialist the Commune actually was. Debate questions Was the Commune a democratic model or a short, stressed emergency? Did Lenin follow Marx or distort him?
Engels: Dialectics, the Family and the State
The second voice of Marxism

Friedrich Engels was Marx's friend, funder and editor, and the author of many ideas now labelled Marxism. He also systematised it, for better or worse. Many critics blame "Engels's dialectics of nature" for the rigid Soviet dogma.
A Manchester mill-owner's son

Engels (1820-95) worked at the family firm in Manchester. His Condition of the Working Class in England (1845) described slums and disease with data. He met Marx in 1844 and co-wrote the German Ideology and the Manifesto . After 1883 he edited volumes 2 and 3 of Capital and led European socialism as its elder statesman.
Dialectics of nature

In Anti-Dühring (1878) and the unfinished Dialectics of Nature (published 1925), Engels held that dialectical laws govern nature as well as history: quantity turns into quality (water boils), opposites interpenetrate, and negation of negation (a seed grows, is eaten, regrows). He used examples from chemistry and Darwin's evolution. Soviet "diamat" built on this.
Family, property and the state

The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State (1884) drew on Lewis Henry Morgan's Ancient Society (1877). Engels proposed that early societies had communal property and kinship, and that private property and the monogamous family arose together: "the world-historical defeat of the female sex". The state arose to manage class conflict. Women's liberation requires entry into public production.
Scientific socialism

In Socialism: Utopian and Scientific (1880), Engels presented socialism as the consequence of two discoveries: the materialist conception of history and surplus value. His 1895 introduction to Marx's Class Struggles in France admitted that barricade uprisings were outdated and praised the German SPD's votes; revisionists later quoted it as support for peaceful reform.
The "Engelsism" debate

After 1883, Engels's simplified versions travelled widely, in Kautsky's hands and then Lenin's ( Materialism and Empirio-criticism , 1909). Soviet science included Lysenko, who rejected modern genetics under Stalin, ruining Soviet biology for decades. In letters of 1890-94, Engels himself warned against crude economic determinism.
Did Engels distort Marx?

Lukács ( History and Class Consciousness , 1923) argued the dialectic belongs to history and society, not nature. Western Marxists (Gramsci, Sartre) agree. Terrell Carver and others claim Engels created "Marxism" as a system that Marx never wrote. Anthropologists have rejected Morgan's unilinear stages; modern research finds more variety in early gender roles. Scientists say nature's laws are not dialectical in any testable sense. Defenders say Engels was candid and an honest populariser.
Family and gender

The Origin was influential for Indian women's movements of the 1970s and for the left's approach to the family. Scholars such as Uma Chakravarti ( Gendering Caste , 2003) stress that caste and patriarchy shape the Indian family in ways the Engelsian scheme did not foresee. Rajani Palme Dutt, a British-Indian communist, wrote India Today (1940), applying Engelsian-Leninist analysis to India. Sections of the Hindu code reform debates (1950s) took up some themes of women's property.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Engels documented the English working class in 1845 and edited Capital after Marx. Dialectics of nature extends the dialectic to the natural world. The Origin (1884) links private property, family and state. Engels shaped the systematic form of "Marxism" and the Second International. Critics blame him for determinism and the unscientific "dialectics of nature". Debate questions Is "Marxism" more Engels's creation than Marx's? Does a gender analysis fit Engels's family account today?
The Second International: Kautsky, Bernstein and Revisionism
Reform or revolution, the first great split

By 1900 socialists had mass parties, newspapers and seats in parliaments. Success posed a question that still divides the left: if workers can win elections and reforms, why make a revolution? The answer split Marxism into social democracy and communism.
The International and the SPD

The Second International was founded in Paris in 1889. Its strongest party was the German SPD (Social Democratic Party), which won about 35% of the vote in 1912 and became the largest party in the Reichstag. The Erfurt Programme (1891), drafted by Kautsky and Bernstein, combined a Marxist goal with a day-to-day reform programme.
Kautsky: "the pope of Marxism"

Karl Kautsky (1854-1938), editor of Die Neue Zeit , was the leading theorist. In The Class Struggle (1892) he argued that capitalism's growth would polarise society and that the party should wait for the crisis while building strength, "a revolutionary party, not a party making revolutions". This is called "centrism". He also held that socialist consciousness comes to workers from intellectuals, an idea Lenin borrowed.
Bernstein's revisionism

Eduard Bernstein (1850-1932) wrote The Preconditions of Socialism (1899), known in English as Evolutionary Socialism . Evidence: the middle class was not disappearing, joint-stock companies spread ownership, wages rose, crises were milder, and democracy offered workers a legal road. He concluded that socialism would come through reform. His line: "the final goal is nothing, the movement is everything." The SPD formally condemned his "revisionism" at Dresden (1903).
Imperialism and the war question

The International debated colonies (Stuttgart, 1907), militarism and the general strike. Its resolutions (a 1907 amendment drafted by Lenin, Luxemburg and Martov) said that if war broke out, socialists must use the crisis to bring down capitalism. In practice, most leaders backed their own governments.
August 1914 and Germany 1918-19

On 4 August 1914 the SPD in the Reichstag voted for war credits, and French and Belgian socialists joined their governments. The International collapsed. After the war, the SPD's Friedrich Ebert led Germany, and in January 1919 his government used the Freikorps to crush the Spartacist uprising; Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht were murdered on 15 January 1919. The left split into SPD and the KPD, and, later, German workers' parties could not stop Hitler in 1933.
Was revisionism right?

Lenin called Kautsky a "renegade" and revisionism a betrayal. Luxemburg said reform cannot be an end in itself. Social democrats point to postwar welfare states in Sweden and Germany as proof Bernstein was largely right: strong unions, universal services and democracy. Critics of the SPD answer that this was won in a unique period and that capital eventually claws back (neoliberal 1980s). Liberals say the welfare state is a capitalist success, not a socialist one.
Social democracy in India

Fabian and Labour ideas reached India: Nehru's "socialistic pattern of society" (Avadi Congress 1955), the Congress Socialist Party (1934, Jayaprakash Narayan, Acharya Narendra Dev, Ram Manohar Lohia), and later the Janata and socialist parties follow the evolutionary road. J.P. described democratic socialism as an alternative to both capitalism and Soviet communism. Left Front governments in West Bengal and Kerala often acted like reformists, though the CPI(M) officially keeps a revolutionary programme.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways The Second International (1889) united mass socialist parties. Kautsky: wait for the crisis; Bernstein: reform is the road. Revisionism was condemned at Dresden (1903) but the SPD practised it. August 1914 broke the International and set the stage for communism. Welfare states are the strongest evidence for Bernstein; the interwar record is the strongest for his critics. Debate questions Is "the movement is everything" a realistic or a defeatist slogan? Did social democracy save capitalism or humanise it?
Rosa Luxemburg: Reform or Revolution
The Marxist who criticised everyone
Rosa Luxemburg (1871-1919) attacked Bernstein, then Lenin, then her own party. Murdered in Berlin in 1919, she is the left's most beloved dissident: a revolutionary who insisted on democracy.
From Poland to Berlin

Born in Zamość, Russian Poland, to a Jewish family, Luxemburg earned a doctorate in Zurich, co-founded the Social Democracy of the Kingdom of Poland, and moved to Germany in 1898. She taught at the SPD party school and was jailed several times, including through the war. She helped found the Spartacus League (1916) and the KPD (December 1918).
Reform or Revolution (1899)

Her pamphlet answered Bernstein. Reforms and revolution are not two methods you pick at a buffet. Unions and parliament are the schooling ground, but capitalism's contradictions will not vanish, so only the conquest of political power ends it. Revisionism, she said, does not choose a slower route to the same goal, but a different goal altogether.
The mass strike

In The Mass Strike, the Political Party and the Trade Unions (1906), after the Russian Revolution of 1905, she argued that mass action grows spontaneously from workers' own experience and cannot be ordered by leaders. Parties and unions should support it rather than control it. This was a challenge to the SPD's cautious officials.
Accumulation and imperialism

The Accumulation of Capital (1913) argued that capitalism needs non-capitalist regions (colonies, peasants) to realise surplus value, so it expands through imperialism and eventually runs out of room. Economists, including Marxists, rejected the underconsumption logic, but the book shaped later dependency theory.
Against Lenin: freedom and the Russian Revolution

In prison in 1918 she wrote The Russian Revolution (published 1922). She backed the Bolsheviks' courage but attacked their dissolving of the Constituent Assembly, terror and suppression of press. "Freedom only for the supporters of the government... is no freedom at all. Freedom is always freedom for the one who thinks differently." Without public life, she said, the soviets would become empty, with only a bureaucracy ruling.
Berlin, January 1919

Luxemburg doubted a rising was timely but joined the Spartacist rising in Berlin; the Freikorps, with SPD government backing, suppressed it. She was beaten and shot on 15 January 1919, her body thrown into the Landwehr Canal. The killers largely escaped punishment. Her death left the German left divided for good.
Weak points

Lenin (1922) conceded she made mistakes but called her an "eagle", while rejecting her spontaneity theory as ineffective without organisation. Economists (Bauer, Bukharin, 1913 onwards) showed her accumulation model has flaws, since capitalists can sell to each other. Historians argue that mass spontaneity failed in Germany 1918-19, because leaderless action gave the Freikorps easy victory. Liberals see in her a moral humanist, but note that she also defended revolutionary violence.
Spontaneity and mass action in India

Luxemburg is less known in Indian communist circles than Lenin, but her ideas resonate with the study of peasant and worker struggles like the Telangana uprising (1946-51) and the Bombay textile strike of 1982, led by Datta Samant outside the established unions. Subaltern historians (Ranajit Guha, Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency , 1983) emphasise the spontaneity and autonomy of insurgents. Her colonial analysis offers a lens for India's "primitive accumulation" debates, notably in land acquisition conflicts.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Reform and revolution are linked; revisionism changes the goal itself. The mass strike arises from workers' experience and not from orders. Accumulation of Capital links imperialism to capitalism's need for outside markets. She backed the Bolsheviks yet insisted on democracy and free debate. She was murdered on 15 January 1919 with SPD government complicity. Debate questions Is spontaneity a strength or a weakness in modern protest movements? Can a revolution be both democratic and defended against counter-revolution?
Anarchism vs Marxism: Bakunin and Kropotkin
The oldest quarrel on the left

Marxists and anarchists agree capitalism and the state oppress, and they agree on a stateless goal. They quarrel about the road: seize the state, or smash it at once? Every later split from Lenin to the Spanish Civil War repeats this argument.
The split in the First International

The International Workingmen's Association (1864) united Marx's followers, Proudhonists and Mikhail Bakunin's Alliance. At The Hague congress (1872), Marx's side expelled Bakunin and moved the General Council to New York, effectively ending it. The next year, anarchists formed the Saint-Imier International.
Bakunin: the state is the enemy

Mikhail Bakunin (1814-76), a Russian aristocrat turned exile, argued in Statism and Anarchy (1873) that the Marxist "People's State" would be rule by a scientific elite. "Take the most radical revolutionary and invest him with absolute power," he warned, "and within a year he will be worse than the Tsar" (a popular paraphrase). He trusted peasants and urban poor, not only industrial workers, and wanted collectivism and federations from below.
Kropotkin: mutual aid

Peter Kropotkin (1842-1921), a Russian prince and geographer, wrote The Conquest of Bread (1892) and Mutual Aid (1902). Against social Darwinism, he argued that cooperation within species is as important as competition. His anarchist communism sketched self-governing communes, with free access to goods and a mix of manual and mental work.
Marxist replies

Marx and Engels, in On Authority (1873) and replies to Bakunin, said anarchists who abolish the state overnight leave workers defenceless against organised capital. The state is needed to break resistance and reorganise production; only afterwards does it wither. They also accused Bakunin of conspiracy and of founding secret groups.
Paris, Russia, Spain, Ukraine

Anarchists took part in the Commune. In Russia, Nestor Makhno's Ukraine (1918-21) was crushed by the Red Army; the Kronstadt sailors' revolt (March 1921) was suppressed. Spain was the biggest test: in July 1936 the CNT-FAI held Barcelona and Catalonia, collectivised industry and farms, and then lost internal fights with the Communists in May 1937 as war went on. Franco won in 1939.
Who was right?

Marxists: anarchism is naive: without an organised force you cannot defeat armies, as Spain shows. Anarchists: every Marxist state became what Bakunin predicted, a bureaucratic elite (Soviet Union, China). Liberals: both underestimate the need for law and checks. Historians: anarchist experiments such as Catalonia (1936-37) were real, but the war pushed policy; accounts differ about food shortages and the CNT's part in coercion. Orwell , in Homage to Catalonia (1938), gave a famous eyewitness view of anarchist Barcelona.
Anarchist strands in India

Gandhi's ideal of Ram Rajya and village self-rule ( gram swaraj ) shared anarchist themes: distrust of the state, voluntary association, means shaping ends. Tolstoy corresponded with Gandhi in 1909-10. Vinoba Bhave and J.P. Narayan's "partyless democracy" and the Total Revolution (1974) echo it. Revolutionaries such as Bhagat Singh read Bakunin, and the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (1928) moved from romantic terror to socialism. Marxists such as M.N. Roy were scornful of Gandhian anarchism.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Marxists and anarchists split at the Hague, 1872. Bakunin feared a new ruling class; Kropotkin stressed mutual aid. Marx held that a transitional state is needed. Spain 1936-39 was the biggest anarchist experiment; it ended in defeat. The record of communist states fits the anarchist warning; the record of anarchists shows organisational weakness. Debate questions Do ends shape means, or can a harsh method be justified by the goal? Could any modern complex economy run without a state?
Lenin: The Vanguard Party
The idea that remade Marxism

Lenin's answer to "how do workers win?" was a tight party of professional revolutionaries. It produced the Bolshevik victory of 1917, and became the model for communist parties worldwide. It also shaped the Soviet one-party state. Few ideas have had more consequences.
Tsarist Russia

Russia in 1900 was an autocracy with a large peasantry, little legal politics and some big modern factories (Putilov in St Petersburg). The Russian Social Democratic Labour Party (RSDLP) formed in 1898. Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov (1870-1924), his brother Alexander executed in 1887 for plotting against the Tsar, became a revolutionary and wrote as "Lenin" from 1901.
What Is To Be Done? (1902)

Lenin argued that workers by themselves develop only "trade-union consciousness": bargaining for wages. Socialist consciousness has to be brought from outside by intellectuals and a vanguard party of full-time revolutionaries, organised under conspiracy conditions in a police state. He was borrowing from Kautsky. The title echoes Chernyshevsky's novel (1863).
Democratic centralism and the 1903 split

At the second RSDLP congress (London, 1903), Lenin wanted a narrow membership of active party workers; Martov wanted a broader one. Lenin's side narrowly won a vote and took the name Bolsheviks (majority), while Martov's were Mensheviks (minority). Democratic centralism : free debate until a decision, then strict discipline for all.
Alliance of workers and peasants

Lenin held that Russia's bourgeoisie was too weak to lead its own revolution. The working class must lead, with the peasantry as ally ( Two Tactics of Social Democracy , 1905). After 1917, the April Theses reorganised the party for a socialist revolution straight away. Mensheviks, following orthodox Marx, held that Russia had to pass through a capitalist stage first.
From 1903 to 1918

The party was small: a few thousand in 1905, about 24,000 in early 1917, and some 240,000 by October 1917. After October 1917 Lenin banned rival socialist parties (1918-21) and, at the Tenth Congress (March 1921), banned factions inside the party. Organising secrecy and discipline made it effective, yet later tools, such as the Cheka (1917), the one-party state and Stalin's general secretaryship (1922), grew from the same logic.
The vanguard under fire

Luxemburg (1904, Organisational Questions ) warned of ultra-centralism: the party's committee would replace the working class. Trotsky in 1904 warned that "the organisation of the party substitutes itself for the party; the Central Committee for the organisation; the dictator for the Central Committee" (a prediction he later regretted). Anarchists saw a new elite. Historians disagree: Lars Lih argues What Is To Be Done? was less authoritarian than its reputation; Leopold Haimson and Robert Service see a line to Stalin. Liberals : it destroys pluralism.
The vanguard in India

Lenin's model shaped the Communist Party of India, formed in 1920 in Tashkent (the CPI claims 1925 at Kanpur). M.N. Roy attended the Second Comintern Congress (1920), where he argued with Lenin over colonial strategy. The party's Meerut Conspiracy Case (1929-33) targeted communist trade unionists. In 1964 the CPI split over the stance towards the Congress; CPI(M) held to a stricter democratic centralism, a feature that critics link to limited internal debate and long leadership terms.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Lenin held workers alone reach trade-union consciousness. The vanguard is a disciplined party of professional revolutionaries. The 1903 split created Bolsheviks and Mensheviks. After 1917 the one-party state and ban on factions followed. Historians still debate whether Stalinism flows from Leninism. Debate questions Is a vanguard compatible with democracy? Was Lenin a faithful interpreter of Marx on revolution?
Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism
Why workers fought each other in 1914

Why did the proletariat of Europe march to war in 1914 instead of rising against it? Lenin's Imperialism (1916) is the answer: capitalism had changed into a new stage of monopolies and colonies, and bought off part of its workers. It also provided the left's way of reading global poverty.
Hobson, Hilferding and war

Lenin wrote in Zurich in 1916, relying on J.A. Hobson's Imperialism (1902) and Rudolf Hilferding's Finance Capital (1910), and on Bukharin. Europe had divided Africa (Berlin Conference 1884-85) and most of Asia. Great powers armed. The pamphlet was subtitled "a popular outline".
Five features

Lenin lists five marks of imperialism: - Concentration of production into monopolies . - Merger of bank and industrial capital into finance capital , ruled by a financial oligarchy. - Export of capital , not just goods. - International monopolist combines dividing the world. - The territorial division of the world among the great powers.
Labour aristocracy

Super-profits from colonies let capitalists pay a layer of workers better, making them conservative: the "labour aristocracy". That explains reformism and the Second International's betrayal of 1914. Engels had noted something similar for Britain. Lenin urged revolutionaries to split from such leaders.
The weakest link and self-determination

War among imperialist powers, Lenin argued, produces crises that allow revolution where the system is weakest: Russia. He also backed national self-determination for colonies (1914 essay, The Right of Nations to Self-Determination ), making anti-colonial movements allies of socialism. The Comintern (1919) and the Baku Congress of the Peoples of the East (1920) followed.
Anti-colonial politics

Leninist anti-imperialism drew in Ho Chi Minh, Mao, and many Asian and African leaders, and created Soviet aid in the Cold War. Yet the USSR itself held an empire: the Baltics were annexed in 1940, Eastern Europe came under Soviet control, and the invasions of Hungary (1956), Czechoslovakia (1968), and Afghanistan (1979) showed the limits of anti-imperial principle. Critics call that "Soviet social-imperialism" (Maoist phrase).
Does the theory hold?

Economists: most capital exports before 1914 went to other rich or settler countries, not to poor colonies; Britain's trade with the colonies was a modest share. Kautsky (1914) said "ultra-imperialism", a peaceful cartel of powers, was possible. Schumpeter (1919) held that imperialism was a relic of pre-capitalist militarism, not capitalism. Historians (Robinson and Gallagher, "Imperialism of Free Trade", 1953) stress strategy and local crises. Post-colonial scholars say Lenin underestimates colonised people's agency and racism. Yet Marxist defenders say the theory predicted the scramble and unequal exchange.
Drain, empire and Indian communism

Lenin's account fits the drain theory of Naoroji and R.C. Dutt. M.N. Roy's thesis in 1920 held that colonial profits sustained European labour. The CPI called Indian independence in 1947 "false" for a time (the Ranadive line of 1948-50), reading the national bourgeoisie as a junior partner of imperialism. Later debates in the "Mode of Production in Indian Agriculture" (1970s) and Prabhat Patnaik's work on neo-colonial finance continue the framework.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Imperialism (1916) links monopoly capitalism and colonial expansion. Five features: monopolies, finance capital, capital export, cartels, territorial division. The labour aristocracy explains reformism. The theory justified anti-colonial alliances and the weakest-link strategy. Critics: capital flows went mostly to rich countries; imperialism is not a necessary stage. Debate questions Is imperialism a feature of capitalism or of states? Does the theory explain modern global inequality?
State and Revolution and 1917
How the revolution actually happened

In 1917 the world's largest country passed from Tsar to a democratic republic to a Bolshevik government in nine months. Lenin's State and Revolution promised a state as simple as the Commune; reality produced the reverse. Understanding the gap is the key to the whole communist story.
Russia at war

By 1917 Russia had lost millions of soldiers in the First World War, food was short and the Tsar had lost the loyalty of his generals. Strikes in Petrograd led to the abdication of Nicholas II on 15 March 1917 (2 March in the old calendar). The Provisional Government continued the war, while workers' and soldiers' soviets (councils) held real power: 'dual power'.
State and Revolution (1917)

Written in hiding in August-September 1917, it reads Marx and Engels on the state. The bourgeois state must be smashed, not captured. In its place: armed workers, officials paid a worker's wage, elected and recallable, as in the Commune. Under communism, administration becomes so simple that "any cook" can do it (a phrase he used elsewhere in 1917). The book ends unfinished as events overtook him.
Peace, Land, Bread; All Power to the Soviets

The April Theses (1917) called for no support for the Provisional Government and for soviet power. Slogans were concrete: peace, land to peasants, bread to cities. The Bolsheviks grew from tens of thousands to several hundred thousand members by autumn and won majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow soviets. Trotsky, head of the Petrograd Soviet's Military Revolutionary Committee, organised the seizure on 25 October (7 November new style).
The decrees and the Constituent Assembly

On 26 October the Congress of Soviets passed the Decree on Peace and the Decree on Land. Elections to the Constituent Assembly, held in November, gave the SRs a majority (about 40% of votes against the Bolsheviks' roughly 24%). The Assembly met on 5 January 1918 and was dissolved by force the next day. The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (March 1918) gave up large territories to Germany.
Gap between promise and practice

Lenin's book promised workers' control; the new state soon built the Cheka (December 1917), the Red Army, a one-party system, and appointed managers over elected factory committees. Civil war (1918-21) justified emergency, but the structures persisted. The Bolsheviks were a minority in the country and ruled in the name of the working class, as Luxemburg had foreseen.
Revolution or coup?

Pipes ( The Russian Revolution , 1990) calls October a coup by a conspiratorial minority. Social historians (Alexander Rabinowitch, Sheila Fitzpatrick) show mass support in the cities and among soldiers, but see a fragile mandate. Mensheviks held that Russia was not ripe. Anarchists point to Kronstadt (1921). Defenders reply that liberals and the SRs failed to end war or give land, so mass opinion turned to the Bolsheviks.
1917 in India

The Russian Revolution reached India through the press and returning exiles. The CPI emerged in 1920-25; Bhagat Singh and the HSRA, Jawaharlal Nehru (who visited Moscow in 1927) and Subhas Bose were influenced. The British banned communism, brought the Peshawar (1922-23) and Kanpur (1924) conspiracy cases. Nehru wrote that the Soviet experiment was a "great adventure", yet he favoured parliamentary democracy for India.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways 1917: Tsar falls in March; Bolsheviks seize power on 25 October. State and Revolution promised a Commune-style state with recallable officials. The Constituent Assembly was dissolved in January 1918 after Bolsheviks won around a quarter of the vote. Cheka and a one-party state emerged soon after. Historians divide between coup and mass revolution. Debate questions Was October 1917 a popular revolution or a coup? Why did a book promising a withering state lead to a powerful one?
War Communism, NEP and the Soviet State
Can you build socialism by decree?

Between 1918 and 1928 the Soviet state tried both extremes: total control of the economy under civil war, then a mixed market economy. The lessons from this decade still run through every debate on planning and markets.
Civil war, 1918-21

The Reds (Bolsheviks) fought the Whites, with foreign intervention by Britain, France, Japan and others, as well as Greens and Ukrainian forces. Estimates of deaths from fighting, terror and disease run to several millions (commonly 7-12 million including famine). The Red Army under Trotsky won by 1920-21.
War Communism

The policy included nationalised industry, grain requisitioning ( prodrazvyorstka ) from peasants, rationing, abolition of private trade, and labour conscription. Some believed it was true communism: money was going to wither. Industrial output collapsed to a fraction of its 1913 level and cities lost half their population as people fled to the countryside.
Revolt and retreat: NEP

Peasant risings (Tambov, 1920-21) and the Kronstadt sailors' revolt (March 1921) alarmed Lenin. At the Tenth Party Congress he replaced requisition with a tax in kind and allowed private trade: the New Economic Policy (NEP). The state held the "commanding heights" (heavy industry, banks, foreign trade). Lenin called it a retreat, "a tactical retreat", but said it was serious and long.
The Soviet state takes shape

The Soviet Union was formally created in December 1922. Lenin's last works include a "Testament" (December 1922) warning that Stalin, as general secretary, had accumulated "unlimited authority" and should be removed. He suffered strokes from 1922 and died on 21 January 1924. The Party also had control of the courts and press; the secret police (Cheka, then GPU) survived.
NEP results and tensions

NEP revived farming: by 1926-27 output approached pre-war levels. Private traders ("Nepmen") grew rich, and a "scissors crisis" (1923) of high industrial and low farm prices hurt peasants. The Soviet debate: Bukharin ("enrich yourselves") backed NEP; the Left Opposition (Preobrazhensky) wanted "primitive socialist accumulation" from peasants to fund industry. The 1927-28 grain-procurement crisis ended the compromise.
What does the decade show?

Hayek and Mises said War Communism showed the impossibility of moneyless planning; Mises had made this argument in 1920. Marxists (Bukharin) defended NEP as the correct "worker-peasant alliance"; Trotskyists said NEP fostered bureaucracy and kulaks. Historians (Orlando Figes, Richard Pipes) stress the human cost of requisitioning and the 1921-22 famine (about 5 million deaths, estimates 5-6 million). Defenders point to the war emergency and to NEP's recovery.
NEP and Indian planning

Indian leaders of the 1930s-50s admired Soviet planning but chose a "mixed economy". The 1956 Industrial Policy Resolution gave the public sector the "commanding heights", a phrase from the NEP debates. The Second Five-Year Plan (1956-61), shaped by P.C. Mahalanobis, put heavy industry first, which has been compared with Preobrazhensky's priority on industrial accumulation. Yet India kept private farms and an open democracy, avoiding the agrarian compulsion of later Soviet history.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways War Communism (1918-21): requisitioning, nationalisation, economic collapse. The Kronstadt and Tambov revolts led to the NEP (March 1921). NEP revived the economy, with the state holding the commanding heights. Lenin's Testament warned against Stalin, who became general secretary in 1922. The 1927-28 grain crisis ended NEP and prepared collectivisation. Debate questions Was NEP a retreat or the correct socialist road? Did War Communism reveal the limits of planning?
Trotsky and Permanent Revolution
The road not taken, or not?

Leon Trotsky is the great "what if" of communism: organiser of the October rising, founder of the Red Army, exiled by Stalin and murdered in Mexico. His theory of permanent revolution and his critique of Soviet bureaucracy are the foundation of all Trotskyist currents. He is also a figure whose own record is disputed.
From Menshevik to Bolshevik

Born Lev Bronstein (1879) in Ukraine, he led the St Petersburg Soviet in 1905, was jailed and exiled, and in 1917 joined the Bolsheviks. He was People's Commissar for Foreign Affairs, then for War (1918-25). After Lenin's death (1924) he lost the power struggle to Stalin, Zinoviev and Kamenev. He was expelled from the party in 1927, exiled to Alma-Ata in 1928, and deported in 1929.
Permanent revolution

In Results and Prospects (1906) Trotsky argued that in backward Russia, the weak bourgeoisie could not complete a democratic revolution. The working class, backed by the peasantry, would have to take power and then go beyond bourgeois tasks to socialist ones. But socialism could not survive in one backward country: the revolution must spread internationally ("permanent"). The Permanent Revolution (1930) generalised this to colonial countries.
Combined and uneven development

Backward countries do not repeat Europe's stages; they leap, combining modern factories with archaic landlordism. This explains the paradox of a proletarian revolution in a peasant country, and anticipates later "dependency" ideas. His History of the Russian Revolution (1930) is a literary masterpiece.
The Revolution Betrayed (1936)

In exile Trotsky called the USSR a degenerated workers' state : property was still nationalised, but a privileged bureaucracy had seized political power. It must be overthrown by a political (not social) revolution, restoring soviet democracy. Stalin's foreign policy and the Moscow Trials (1936-38) were symptoms. He founded the Fourth International (1938).
Exile and murder

Trotsky moved to Turkey, France, Norway and Mexico (1937). Stalin accused him in show trials of wrecking and treason; most of the Old Bolsheviks were executed. Ramón Mercader, an NKVD agent, struck him with an ice axe on 20 August 1940; he died the next day. Trotskyist groups later formed small but influential parties (Sri Lanka's LSSP, Bolivia, the UK's Militant, France's LCR).
Hero or hypocrite?

Stalinists called him a wrecker. Anarchists point to his role in crushing Kronstadt in 1921 and in militarising labour (1920). Historians (Isaac Deutscher's 3-volume biography, 1954-63) treat him sympathetically; Robert Service (2009) and Pierre Broué disagree. Liberals and Mensheviks : his own plans for "militarising labour" and 1920-21 repression show he shared Lenin's methods. Theory : critics say that "degenerated workers' state" is ad hoc and cannot account for the survival of the USSR for decades, or for China and Eastern Europe.
Trotskyism in India

Indian Trotskyists were few: the Bolshevik-Leninist Party of India (1942), the Revolutionary Communist Party, and the Lanka Sama Samaja Party in Sri Lanka (1935), which had large influence there. In India, the Left's main debates, such as the character of the national bourgeoisie and "permanent revolution" in an agrarian country, reflect Trotsky versus Stalin, as does the debate whether Indian democracy can be socialised. The Fourth International's Indian ties were weak.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Permanent revolution: backward countries' workers must go beyond a bourgeois revolution and link with international revolution. Combined and uneven development explains leaps. The USSR was, for Trotsky, a degenerated workers' state needing political revolution. Stalin's agent murdered him in 1940. Critics note his role in Kronstadt and his own authoritarian record. Debate questions Would Trotsky's Russia have been less violent than Stalin's? Is the theory of a degenerated workers' state convincing?
Stalin: Socialism in One Country
The man who built the system

Joseph Stalin (1878-1953) ruled the USSR for about 30 years. His doctrine of "socialism in one country" justified building a state, then an empire. Whether Stalinism is Marxism's tragic outcome or its betrayal is the oldest dispute on the left.
Rise of a bureaucrat

Born Ioseb Jughashvili in Gori, Georgia, a seminary student turned bank-robber and Bolshevik organiser. He became general secretary in April 1922. After Lenin's death in 1924 he allied first with Zinoviev and Kamenev against Trotsky, then with Bukharin against them, and finally broke Bukharin (1928-29).
Socialism in one country

In late 1924 Stalin argued that the USSR could build socialism alone, without waiting for revolution in the West. Against Trotsky's permanent revolution it gave a patriotic goal and reassurance to a tired party. Bukharin supported it as a way to keep NEP. In practice it meant industrial drives, party loyalty and nationalism.
Marxism-Leninism, "diamat" and the cult

Stalin wrote Foundations of Leninism (1924), and the Short Course history of the Party (1938), which became the compulsory canon. Dialectical and historical materialism were reduced to a catechism. Culture was brought under "socialist realism" (1934). Lysenko gained control of biology. A cult of personality presented Stalin as the genius leader.
Party, police and terror

By 1929 he held supreme power. The Great Terror of 1936-38 followed the murder of Kirov (December 1934). Show trials convicted Zinoviev, Kamenev, Bukharin and others. About 680,000 were shot in 1937-38 by the usual count of recorded executions; many more died in camps. The army leadership was purged in 1937. Nations were deported: Chechens, Crimean Tatars, Volga Germans in the 1940s.
War, empire and 1945

The Nazi-Soviet Pact (August 1939) was followed by the German invasion of June 1941. The Soviet Union lost about 27 million people (the usual estimate). It defeated Germany in 1945 and installed communist governments across Eastern Europe. Stalin's victory gave the system legitimacy, and Soviet prestige abroad soared. He died on 5 March 1953.
Leninism, or betrayal?

Trotskyists : Stalinism betrayed Lenin through bureaucracy. Liberals and Cold War historians (Richard Pipes, Robert Conquest, The Great Terror , 1968): continuous with Lenin's one-party rule. Revisionists (J. Arch Getty, Sheila Fitzpatrick) stress chaos, popular participation and the central role of local officials. Maoists defended him as "70% good". Anarchists : the state grew, not withered. Western Marxists : Stalin made Marxism a state ideology.
Stalin and the Indian left

The CPI followed Soviet lines: it supported the war after June 1941 and called it a "People's War", opposing the Quit India Movement of 1942, which cost it popularity. After Stalin's death in 1953, CPI leaders mourned. Stalinist structure shaped the Indian party: central committee control, expulsions, loyalty to Moscow. The Soviet Union's support in the UN and with steel plants (Bhilai, 1955) shaped India's ties with it. Many Indian Marxists, such as Romesh Thapar, later became critics.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Socialism in one country (1924) replaced waiting for world revolution. Stalin built a party-police state with a cult and a compulsory ideology. The Great Terror (1936-38) killed about 680,000 in executions, with many more dead in camps. The USSR won the Second World War at the cost of about 27 million dead. Debate: Stalinism as continuation or betrayal of Leninism. Debate questions Was socialism in one country a necessity or a retreat? Is the Stalin question the same as the Lenin question?
Collectivisation, Industrialisation and the Gulag
Industrial leap and human cost

The first Five-Year Plan (1928) and forced collectivisation changed the Soviet Union from a peasant to an industrial power in a decade. They also caused a famine that killed millions and built a prison-camp system. This is the central moral test case for the whole communist experiment.
The grain crisis

In 1927-28 peasants withheld grain from the state because prices were low. Stalin responded with "extraordinary measures" seizing grain, ending NEP. The Plan's aim, he said in 1931, was to catch up: "We are fifty or a hundred years behind the advanced countries. We must make good this lag in ten years."
Rapid industrialisation

The Plans prioritised steel, coal, machines. Magnitogorsk and the Dnieper dam rose. Output grew fast (official numbers are inflated; Western estimates still show a very high growth, around 5-6% a year in the 1930s). Industrial workers rose from some 11 million to over 20 million by 1940. Workers had low wages and housing, and harsh discipline; Stakhanovism (1935) glorified record output.
Collectivisation and "dekulakisation"

From late 1929 peasants were pushed into collective farms ( kolkhozy ), and "kulaks" (supposedly rich peasants) were deported or killed: about 1.8 million deported in 1930-31. Peasants slaughtered livestock rather than hand it over. By 1937 about 93% of households were collectivised. The state procured grain at fixed low prices and the countryside financed industry.
Famine and Holodomor

The famine of 1932-33 killed about 5.5 to 8.7 million in the Soviet Union by various estimates, with some 3.5 to 3.9 million in Ukraine and about 1.5 million in Kazakhstan (where roughly a third of Kazakhs died). The Holodomor in Ukraine is recognised as genocide by many parliaments; historians (Robert Conquest, Timothy Snyder, Anne Applebaum) hold that Stalin's policy was intentionally harsh toward Ukraine, while others (R.W. Davies, Stephen Wheatcroft) see mainly a disastrous result of policy and ideology, not a plan to kill Ukrainians as such. All agree that grain exports continued and relief was withheld.
The Gulag

GULAG, the Chief Administration of Camps, ran forced labour in Siberia, Kolyma, the Arctic and Central Asia. About 18 million passed through camps and colonies from 1930 to 1953; some 1.5 to 1.7 million died in them, by archival counts. Solzhenitsyn's The Gulag Archipelago (1973) made the system known to the world. Inmates built canals, railways and mines. Forced labour made up only a small portion of the economy, historians argue.
Balance sheet

The USSR industrialised in time to build the tanks and planes that beat Germany. Yet the countryside was devastated, yields fell for years and agriculture stayed poor to the end. In total, 1930-53 excess deaths from famine, terror, camps and deportations are estimated by historians at around 6 to 9 million (lower) up to 15 to 20 million (higher). No consensus exists on the larger numbers.
Was the leap necessary?

Defenders say the threat of invasion left no time and that other late industrialisers also paid heavy costs. Critics: NEP could have yielded industrialisation with fewer deaths (Bukharin's line); Japan, the US and Britain did not need mass famine. Economists (Alec Nove) argue that the system built "extensive growth" and could not shift to efficiency. Conquest/Applebaum : ideology plus terror. Davies/Wheatcroft : error and rush, but also ideology. Marxists ask whether this is socialism at all.
The Soviet model and India

India's Five-Year Plans (from 1951) borrowed the name and some of the practice but kept private land and democracy. Nehru praised Soviet industrial speed yet rejected collectivisation; the Nagpur Congress resolution (1959) proposed cooperative farming and was dropped. The Bengal famine of 1943 (about 2-3 million dead) is a reminder that famine was also colonial policy, and Amartya Sen's work ( Poverty and Famines , 1981) argues that democracy and a free press prevent famines, citing Soviet and Chinese experience.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways First Five-Year Plan (1928) drove heavy industry. Collectivisation: about 1.8 million deportations and then famine in 1932-33. Famine deaths: roughly 5.5 to 8.7 million, with disagreement over intent. Gulag: about 18 million passed through, with 1.5 to 1.7 million deaths in custody.
