Debate: a necessary leap or an avoidable catastrophe? Debate questions Can economic growth justify mass death? Does Sen's thesis show democracy prevents famine?
Khrushchev, De-Stalinisation and the Thaw
When the system admitted its crimes

In February 1956 the leader of the Soviet Communist Party denounced Stalin to the party's own delegates. It shook the world communist movement more than any Western attack. The episode asks: can a regime reform itself without losing its legitimacy?
Succession struggle

Stalin died on 5 March 1953. Beria, the police chief, was arrested in June and executed in December 1953. Nikita Khrushchev, a Ukrainian-based party boss, won the contest to be First Secretary (September 1953) and by 1957 defeated the "Anti-Party Group" (Molotov, Malenkov, Kaganovich). He was Soviet leader until October 1964.
The Secret Speech (1956)

On 25 February 1956, at a closed session of the 20th Congress, Khrushchev spoke of Stalin's "cult of the individual", the terror of 1937-38, wrongly executed Party members, mistakes in the war, and deportations of nations. He blamed Stalin and the cult, not the system. The text leaked and was published by the US State Department in June 1956. It was not published in the USSR until 1989.
Thaw and reforms

Millions were released from the camps, many rehabilitated. Censorship loosened: Solzhenitsyn's One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich appeared in 1962, with Khrushchev's approval. Yevtushenko, the "Thaw" poets and new films flourished. Khrushchev launched the Virgin Lands programme (1954), housing construction (the khrushchevki ), and "peaceful coexistence" with the West. Sputnik (1957) and Gagarin (1961) boosted prestige.
Limits: Hungary, Pasternak and Cuba

The Thaw was limited. Soviet tanks crushed the Hungarian revolution in November 1956 (about 2,500 Hungarians and 700 Soviet troops killed). Boris Pasternak was forced to refuse the Nobel Prize (1958) over Doctor Zhivago . Novocherkassk workers' protest was suppressed with shooting in 1962 (at least 26 killed). The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 brought the world close to nuclear war. Khrushchev also persecuted churches.
Fall and consequences

Reforms like the sovnarkhoz regional councils (1957) and the Virgin Lands campaign gave mixed results; a poor harvest in 1963 forced grain imports. His colleagues removed him in October 1964. The speech had global effects: the world communist movement split; Mao saw it as revisionist, leading to the Sino-Soviet split (open by 1960-63); many Western communists left parties after 1956.
Truth-telling or self-protection?

Dissidents (Roy Medvedev, who wrote Let History Judge , 1971) welcomed it but said it was too limited. Solzhenitsyn called it a half-truth. Maoists saw it as the start of capitalist restoration. Historians point out that Khrushchev himself had signed death lists in the 1930s, so the speech was partly self-protective. Western left was split: E.P. Thompson and others left the British party, founding the New Left. Defenders : it freed millions and made later reform possible.
Impact on Indian communism

The speech deepened the CPI's internal divisions, which ended in the 1964 split into the CPI and CPI(M). The Sino-Soviet quarrel mapped onto the Indian party: pro-Moscow versus pro-Beijing wings, intensified by the 1962 India-China war, during which many CPI leaders were jailed. Nehru took Soviet aid and technology, and Khrushchev and Bulganin visited India in 1955. India also received Soviet backing on Kashmir at the UN. Ivan Denisovich and other works were translated into several Indian languages.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Secret Speech (25 Feb 1956) denounced Stalin's cult and terror. Thaw: camps emptied, censorship eased, literature bloomed. Limits: Hungary 1956, Pasternak, Novocherkassk. The speech led to the Sino-Soviet split and a crisis for communist parties abroad. Critics: it blamed the man, not the system. Debate questions Could the system have reformed itself? Did the Secret Speech save or weaken communism?
Brezhnev, Stagnation and Gorbachev's Reforms
Slow decay, then sudden change

After Khrushchev, the Soviet Union offered 18 years of stability and decline, then six years of dramatic reform that ended in collapse. The sequence is the key case for whether communism can be reformed.
Order after chaos

Leonid Brezhnev led from 1964 to 1982. His rule is called the "era of stagnation". Stable cadres, a large military and rising living standards in the 1960s-70s coexisted with falling growth. The oil boom after 1973 papered over weakness. Crackdowns on dissidents: Sinyavsky and Daniel trial (1966), the Prague Spring invasion (August 1968), and the Brezhnev Doctrine of limited sovereignty.
Stagnation

Soviet growth rates fell from above 5% to near 2% by the early 1980s (Western estimates). Labour productivity lagged; agriculture needed imports of grain; the shortage economy (János Kornai's term, 1980) produced queues and a black market. Life expectancy for men stopped rising and fell. Defence took perhaps 15-20% of GDP. Corruption and a ageing leadership (the "gerontocracy") of Brezhnev, Andropov and Chernenko followed.
Gorbachev: perestroika and glasnost

Mikhail Gorbachev (b. 1931), General Secretary from March 1985, introduced perestroika (restructuring: the 1987 Law on State Enterprise, cooperatives from 1988), glasnost (openness: free discussion, release of prisoners like Sakharov in 1986), and democratisation (competitive elections to the Congress of People's Deputies, March 1989). Abroad, "new thinking" ended the arms race and the Brezhnev Doctrine; arms control treaties followed (INF Treaty, 1987).
Loosening the grip

Gorbachev meant to renew socialism, "more democracy, more socialism". Instead, glasnost let people publish the history of Stalin's crimes, expose Chernobyl (April 1986), and demand national independence. In 1990 Article 6, guaranteeing the Party's monopoly, was repealed. Boris Yeltsin's election as Russian president in June 1991 gave a rival power centre.
Outcome

Reforms disrupted the old planned economy without creating a working market. Output fell, shortages spread, and the budget collapsed with falling oil prices. In 1989 the Eastern European regimes fell, mostly without Soviet intervention. In August 1991 hardliners tried a coup and failed. The USSR was dissolved on 25-26 December 1991. Gorbachev won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990.
Reform from within

Reformers (Gorbachev, Alexander Yakovlev) argue that without glasnost the economy could not be fixed. Hardliners say he destroyed an order he could not replace. Economists (Anders Åslund) say the sequence was wrong: political opening before a market. China analysts contrast Deng's economic reform with political control, a better path. Stephen Kotkin ( Armageddon Averted , 2001) shows how the system lost its self-belief. Marxists argue that bureaucracy, not socialism, collapsed.
The Soviet partner

India's ties with the USSR were close: the Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation (August 1971) preceded the Bangladesh war; the USSR was India's main arms supplier and rupee-trade partner. Brezhnev visited in 1973 and Gorbachev in 1986 and 1988. India's abstention on Afghanistan in 1980 was resented in the West. The loss of this partner, plus India's own balance-of-payments crisis in 1991, is one background to the 1991 liberalisation under Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Brezhnev era (1964-82): order, military might and slow decay. Gorbachev (from 1985): perestroika, glasnost, democratisation. Reform loosened the Party's monopoly (Article 6 repealed 1990). The USSR dissolved in December 1991. Debate: was reform doomed, or was the sequence wrong? Debate questions Could Gorbachev have saved the Union? Is the Chinese path the lesson of 1991?
Why the Soviet Union Collapsed
The question every theory must answer

A superpower with nuclear weapons and 15 republics dissolved in 1991 with little fighting at the centre. Almost nobody forecast it. Why it fell decides whether communism was doomed by its design or killed by choices and accidents.
The year of falling dominoes

1989: Poland's Solidarity won the June elections; the Berlin Wall opened on 9 November; Czechoslovakia (the Velvet Revolution), Bulgaria and Romania followed; Ceausescu was shot in December. In 1990, the Baltics moved toward independence. In 1991 the August coup failed, and Ukraine voted for independence on 1 December (over 90%). The Belovezha Accords of 8 December ended the Union; Gorbachev resigned on 25 December.
Economic explanations

Growth slowed from the 1970s. Planning could build steel, but not efficient consumer goods or software; innovation lagged in the computer age. Oil revenue fell when prices dropped in 1985-86. Military spending, supporting Cuba, Vietnam and Afghanistan, was a burden. Hayek and Mises's "calculation problem" and Kornai's "soft budget constraint" explain why firms did not respond to signals.
Political and ideological explanations

The Party lost belief in itself. Glasnost exposed its crimes and eroded legitimacy. Stephen Kotkin argues the system was brittle, without legitimate means for succession and correction. Nationalism in the republics (Baltics, Armenia, Georgia, Ukraine) became the main force that broke the Union; Yeltsin's Russia in 1991 undercut the centre. Elites, especially the nomenklatura, saw more benefit from privatising assets than defending socialism.
Agency versus structure

Some stress structure: a system that could not be reformed. Others stress contingency: different choices (a China-style economic reform first, no Chernobyl, a faster Gorbachev) might have saved it. The Afghan war (1979-89, with around 15,000 Soviet dead and a larger number of Afghan dead) and Reagan's arms race are cited by some but are overrated by many historians, who see internal causes as primary.
What came after

The 1990s brought shock therapy, hyperinflation (1992 prices rose about 2,500%), and rapid privatisation to oligarchs. GDP fell by roughly 40% over the decade, and male life expectancy dropped to about 57-58 years in 1994. Wars followed in Chechnya (1994-96 and 1999-). Putin's rule from 2000 restored order and an authoritarian state. Eastern Europe split: Poland and the Czech Republic prospered, Ukraine and Moldova stayed poorer.
Competing verdicts

Liberals and the Right : it proves central planning can't work. Left critics : Stalinist bureaucracy, not socialism; Western shock therapy worsened the damage (Stephen Cohen, Naomi Klein). Trotskyists foretold it in 1936. Conservative historians (Richard Pipes) see inherent illegitimacy. Archie Brown says Gorbachev's choices made the difference. Public opinion polls in Russia show nostalgia: about half regret the collapse. China watchers : a different sequence worked there.
1991 in India and the Indian left

The collapse was a shock to the Indian left, which had admired the Soviet Union. It coincided with India's 1991 reforms, which curtailed licensing, and lessened the Left's intellectual authority. The CPI(M) concluded that the USSR's failure was one of implementation (errors, loss of party leadership) and not of socialism, and the party started to recognise the role of markets in West Bengal (the 2006-07 industrialisation drive, Singur and Nandigram). India lost its main trade and arms partner and recast ties with Russia and the US.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways The USSR collapsed in 1991 after the 1989 revolutions in Eastern Europe. Economic stagnation, loss of Party belief and national movements combined. Structural versus contingent explanations remain open. The 1990s brought hardship and oligarchic privatisation. Verdicts range from "planning cannot work" to "Stalinism, not socialism, failed". Debate questions Was collapse inevitable? What does 1991 prove about socialism as a whole?
Lukács: Class Consciousness and Reification
The birth of Western Marxism

After 1917, Marxism in Western Europe took a philosophical turn. Georg Lukács's History and Class Consciousness (1923) is the founding book. It restored Hegel and the dialectic and gave a language for why workers might not revolt.
A Hungarian aristocrat among Bolsheviks

Born in Budapest (1885) into a wealthy Jewish family, Lukács wrote on literature ( Theory of the Novel , 1916). He joined the Hungarian Communist Party in 1918 and served as a commissar in the short-lived Hungarian Soviet Republic (March-August 1919). In exile in Vienna he wrote the essays of 1919-23 collected as History and Class Consciousness . The Comintern denounced the book in 1924.
Marxism is a method

In "What is Orthodox Marxism?", Lukács says orthodoxy refers to method , not to any particular doctrine: the dialectic and the viewpoint of totality . Facts only have meaning within the whole society. This was a break with the economism of the Second International.
Reification

Building on Capital 's commodity fetishism and Weber's rationalisation, Lukács argued that in capitalism, human relations take on a "phantom objectivity": social relations seem like things with their own laws. The worker's labour becomes a measurable, interchangeable quantity; bureaucracy, law, even the sciences treat the world as fixed facts. Reification thus affects thinking itself, not just the factory.
Class consciousness and the party

The proletariat, since it is reduced to a commodity, can grasp the whole of society as the "identical subject-object" of history. "Imputed" class consciousness is what workers would feel if they understood their real position. The Party is the organised form of that consciousness. Lukács backed Leninism in this book, which was an uneasy marriage.
Later life

In the 1920s Lukács bowed to Comintern criticism and disowned the book (1930s). In exile in Moscow he turned to literary criticism, defending realism (Balzac, Tolstoy) against modernism, and later the Hungarian government. He was minister of culture in Imre Nagy's government in 1956, deported to Romania after the Soviet invasion, returned in 1957 and died in 1971. In 1967 he wrote a new preface criticising the book as "Hegelian".
Hegel in Marx's clothing?

Soviet Marxists (Zinoviev, Bukharin) called it idealist. Althusser thought it historicist and humanist. Adorno said the claim that the proletariat is subject-object is a myth: the worker is also integrated by capitalism. Analytical Marxists find the argument obscure. Liberals see "imputed consciousness" as licence for a party to override real workers' opinion. Defenders : it explains passivity and the power of ideology better than economism.
Reification and Indian Marxism

Lukács was read in India mainly by literary critics and scholars of the Progressive Writers' Association (founded 1936). His realism shaped debate about Premchand and Mulk Raj Anand. Reification suits critiques of caste hierarchy, in which persons become fixed categories. Indian Marxist theory in the 1970s-80s, for example in the work of Sudipta Kaviraj and the Subaltern Studies group, engages "Western Marxism", though mostly Gramsci instead.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways History and Class Consciousness (1923) founded Western Marxism. Orthodoxy means method: dialectic and totality. Reification: social relations appear as things. Class consciousness is "imputed" and carried by the Party. Critics: Hegelian idealism and justification for party authority. Debate questions Does reification explain consumer culture and social media? Can a party know workers' interests better than workers?
Gramsci: Hegemony and the War of Position
Why do the ruled consent?

If capitalism is unjust, why do workers not simply revolt? Antonio Gramsci's answer: because rule rests on consent as well as force. His concept of hegemony is now used by historians, political scientists and activists far beyond Marxism.
Sardinia, Turin, prison

Born in Sardinia (1891), small and sickly, Gramsci studied in Turin, edited L'Ordine Nuovo (1919-20), and backed the factory councils movement. He co-founded the Italian Communist Party (1921) and led it from 1924. Mussolini's regime arrested him in November 1926; the prosecutor said, "we must stop this brain from functioning for twenty years". He wrote 33 notebooks in prison (1929-35) and died in 1937, a few days after release from prison, aged 46.
Hegemony

In the Prison Notebooks (published 1948-51), hegemony is leadership by consent: a class rules when its worldview becomes common sense through schools, churches, press, family and culture, together forming civil society . Coercion (the state in the narrow sense) stays in reserve. "State = political society + civil society, hegemony protected by the armour of coercion."
War of manoeuvre and war of position

In Russia, the state was everything and civil society "primordial and gelatinous", so a frontal assault ( war of manoeuvre ) could win. In the West, civil society is a system of trenches and fortresses, so the left needs a long war of position : building alternative institutions, culture and alliances, before seizing power. This is read as a justification for democratic, gradual strategy.
Organic intellectuals and the historic bloc

Every class creates its organic intellectuals who give it awareness: factory technicians, journalists, union leaders. Traditional intellectuals (priests, professors) claim independence but serve the old order. A historic bloc unites classes around a common project; Gramsci worried about the "Southern Question": northern workers must ally with southern peasants. "Pessimism of the intellect, optimism of the will" is his slogan, borrowed from Romain Rolland.
Eurocommunism, cultural studies, Latin America

Gramsci inspired Togliatti's Italian road to socialism and Eurocommunism, the New Left, Stuart Hall's cultural studies, Laclau and Mouffe, and Latin American politics (Evo Morales's MAS in Bolivia). Edward Said used hegemony to describe Orientalism. Political parties of the right also borrowed it: the "culture war" strategy of intellectuals in the 1970s and the New Right drew on Gramscian ideas, a point made by commentators.
Limits of the concept

Orthodox Marxists say it dilutes class and the economy. Perry Anderson (1976) found Gramsci ambiguous about civil society and the state. Liberals say consent in democracies is real, not false consciousness. Historians warn about "Gramsci for everyone" and about relying on fragmentary, coded prison writings written under censorship. Althusser found a historicist streak. Critics from the left ask whether a war of position never ends and never delivers.
Subaltern and hegemony

Gramsci's notion of "subaltern classes" was borrowed by Ranajit Guha and the Subaltern Studies collective (1982), who wrote history from below. Partha Chatterjee used hegemony in Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986). Debate: the Indian National Congress gained hegemony in the freedom struggle by uniting classes under bourgeois leadership, which Gramscians call "passive revolution", a phrase Chatterjee applied to India. The BJP-RSS cultural project is often analysed as a hegemony struggle.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Hegemony: rule by consent through civil society, with force in reserve. War of manoeuvre versus war of position. Organic intellectuals and the historic bloc. Prison Notebooks, 1929-35, published after the war. Critics: concept is vague and dilutes class. Debate questions Is culture or the economy the main battlefield? Does hegemony explain right-wing populism?
The Frankfurt School: Adorno, Horkheimer, Marcuse
Marxism after defeat

When the working class failed to make revolution in the West, and Hitler, Stalin and mass consumer culture arrived, a group of German-Jewish intellectuals asked why. Their "critical theory" shaped the New Left and modern cultural criticism.
The Institute for Social Research

Founded in Frankfurt in 1923-24, the Institute under Max Horkheimer (director from 1930) fled the Nazis in 1933 to Geneva, then New York (Columbia) in 1934, and returned to Frankfurt in 1950. Members: Theodor Adorno, Herbert Marcuse, Walter Benjamin, Erich Fromm, Friedrich Pollock, Leo Löwenthal. Later generation: Jürgen Habermas.
Critical theory

In Traditional and Critical Theory (1937), Horkheimer contrasted theory that describes society as given with theory that aims at human emancipation. It combined Marx, Freud (to explain why people desire their own domination) and Weber. Fromm and Adorno's team studied The Authoritarian Personality (1950).
Dialectic of Enlightenment

Horkheimer and Adorno's Dialectic of Enlightenment (1944-47) argued that reason, meant to free humanity from myth, turned into instrumental reason , a tool of domination of nature and people. Auschwitz was not a relapse but the dark side of Enlightenment. The chapter on the culture industry : film, radio and pop music standardise tastes and pacify the masses.
Marcuse: one-dimensional man

One-Dimensional Man (1964) argued that advanced capitalism absorbs opposition via consumption and "repressive tolerance"; false needs replace real ones. The revolution might come from outsiders: students, minorities, the Third World poor. Eros and Civilization (1955) argued for liberated sexuality. He became a guru of the 1968 students' movement. Habermas later turned to rational communication in the public sphere ( Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere , 1962).
1968 and after

The Frankfurt thinkers were uneasy with student activism: Adorno called police on occupying students in 1969 and died that August; Habermas warned of "left fascism". The School's ideas influenced media studies, feminism, and the critique of consumerism. Practical politics was weak: Horkheimer drifted to conservatism.
Elitist and pessimistic?

Orthodox Marxists (Lukács called them the "Grand Hotel Abyss") accused them of retreat into theory. Liberals and Popper see irrationalism and neglect of democracy. Cultural studies (Stuart Hall) found the culture-industry thesis condescending towards audiences. Habermas found it self-undermining: if reason is dominated, on what basis does it criticise? Feminists : neglect of gender. Empirical challengers: working people actively interpret mass culture.
Critical theory in India

Frankfurt ideas arrived in Indian universities through literary, film and media studies. Ashis Nandy's critique of the modern state and science and Dipesh Chakrabarty's "provincialising Europe" (2000) share critical suspicion of Enlightenment universalism. Debates on commercial Hindi cinema and television's impact on public culture use the "culture industry" framework, while Habermas's public sphere is used for questions about Indian media and civil society.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways The Frankfurt School combined Marx, Freud and Weber to study why capitalism lasts. Dialectic of Enlightenment: reason became domination. Culture industry pacifies mass audiences. Marcuse looked to outsiders for revolt in a one-dimensional society. Critics: elitism, pessimism, and the lack of a political strategy. Debate questions Do social media and streaming prove the culture-industry thesis? Is Enlightenment reason the problem or the solution?
Althusser and Structural Marxism
Marxism as a science, without a subject

Louis Althusser tried to rescue Marxism from both Stalinist dogma and humanist sentiment. He made ideology, "interpellation" and the "break" into household words in theory seminars. His own life ended in tragedy, which colours how his work is read.
Paris, the École Normale

Born in Algeria (1918), Althusser was a prisoner of war (1940-45), a Communist from 1948, and a teacher at the École Normale Supérieure in Paris. After 1956 and the Sino-Soviet split, he sought a Marxism that was neither Stalinist nor humanist. For Marx and Reading Capital (both 1965) made him famous. In 1980 he strangled his wife Hélène Rytmann and was declared unfit to stand trial; he died in 1990.
The epistemological break

Althusser divides Marx's work: a young humanist and Hegelian (to 1845), then a scientific Marx from the German Ideology onwards, with the break complete in Capital . The early Marx's "man" and "alienation" are ideological; the mature Marx studies structures: modes of production, classes, relations.
Structure, overdetermination and the process without a subject

History is "a process without a subject": people are bearers of structures. A revolution results from the overdetermination of several contradictions in a conjuncture (Russia 1917), not a single economic contradiction. The economy is determinant "in the last instance", but "the lonely hour of the last instance never comes". The levels (economic, political, ideological) have relative autonomy.
Ideological State Apparatuses

In "Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses" (1970) he distinguishes the Repressive State Apparatus (army, police) from Ideological State Apparatuses (school, church, family, media). Their function: reproduce the relations of production. Ideology "interpellates" individuals as subjects, like a policeman calling "Hey, you!" and the person turning around.
Influence and fall

His students included Balibar, Rancière, Poulantzas, Badiou and Macherey. Structuralist Marxism shaped sociology and film theory, and the study of the state (Poulantzas). In Britain, E.P. Thompson attacked it in The Poverty of Theory (1978). After 1968 and the invasions of Czechoslovakia, the approach lost ground as post-structuralists and "new philosophers" turned away from Marxism, and his personal tragedy ended his public life.
Too structural, too abstract

E.P. Thompson : it is "Stalinism at the level of theory", lacking human agency. Humanists (Sartre's circle): where are people? Analytical Marxists (Cohen, Elster): obscure and unfalsifiable. Historians : the "break" is overstated since Marx kept alienation themes in Grundrisse and Capital . Activists : if ideology is everywhere and unavoidable, how can anyone resist? Defenders : it explains how education and media reproduce class, as Bourdieu showed in sociology.
Ideological apparatuses and Indian schooling

The concept of ideological apparatuses is used by Indian scholars to analyse textbooks, schooling and media, including the history-textbook controversies and NCERT revisions. Krishna Kumar's work on curriculum ( Political Agenda of Education , 1991) reflects a related approach. Caste may be understood as an ideology reproduced through family and ritual, a discussion in Ambedkar and Gail Omvedt's writings. Althusser also influenced Indian film theory and the Mode of Production debate, where analysts used his notion of articulation of modes of production.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Althusser read Marx as a scientist of structures, with a break from the humanist early work. History is a process without a subject; overdetermination replaces simple economic causation. Ideological State Apparatuses reproduce class society; ideology interpellates subjects. Thompson and humanists criticised his neglect of agency. His influence extends to sociology, media and state theory. Debate questions Do individuals matter in history, or only structures? Is the idea of an epistemological break credible?
Sartre, Existentialism and Marxism
Freedom meets history

Jean-Paul Sartre asked what the 20th century's hardest question implies for Marxism: if people are radically free, how can history have laws? His attempt to fuse existentialism and Marxism, and his flawed political choices, make him the great test of the intellectual as revolutionary.
From café philosopher to fellow traveller

Sartre (1905-80) wrote Being and Nothingness (1943) in occupied Paris. After 1945 he turned to politics: Les Temps Modernes (founded 1945 with Simone de Beauvoir and Merleau-Ponty), support for the Communist Party from 1952, break after Hungary (1956), a refusal of the Nobel Prize (1964), and alignment with Maoist students in 1968-70.
Existence precedes essence

Existentialism is a Humanism (1946) holds that people have no fixed nature: they make themselves through choices; they are "condemned to be free". Evasion of freedom is bad faith . This seems opposed to Marx's emphasis on structures, yet Sartre linked the two through the idea of situated freedom.
Critique of Dialectical Reason (1960)

Sartre calls Marxism "the unsurpassable philosophy of our time" but says it lacks a theory of the individual. Scarcity creates relations of seriality (people queuing for a bus are isolated), and in crisis they form groups-in-fusion (the storming of the Bastille), which then harden into institutions. His "progressive-regressive method" combines the structure and the personal project (his study of Flaubert).
Commitment and violence

In "What is Literature?" (1947) he demanded that writers be engagé , committed. He backed Algerian independence and wrote a preface to Fanon's The Wretched of the Earth (1961), defending the violence of the colonised. He also accompanied the French Communist Party for a time ( The Communists and Peace , 1952-54) and described anti-communists as "rats". Later he condemned the invasions of Hungary and Czechoslovakia.
1968 and the end

Sartre sold the Maoist paper La Cause du peuple on the street (1970) and was arrested, then released on De Gaulle's orders ("you don't arrest Voltaire"). He visited Cuba (1960, praising Castro), the USSR, and China (1955), often with generous eyes. His funeral in April 1980 drew about 50,000 people.
The intellectual's failures

Camus broke with him (1952) over the Soviet camps; The Rebel (1951) rejected revolutionary violence. Raymond Aron ( The Opium of the Intellectuals , 1955) mocked fellow-travelling. Merleau-Ponty broke from him over Korea (1950). Althusser and structuralists (Lévi-Strauss) attacked his humanism. Moral critics note his silence about the camps until 1956 and his later excuse. Defenders : he changed his mind, took risks, and tried to give Marxism a lived dimension.
Existentialism and Indian thought

Sartre's writings reached India in the 1950s-70s through literature and politics. Hindi and Bengali modernist writers (Agyeya, Nirmal Verma, Jibanananda Das's circle) were influenced by existentialist themes. Fanon's influence on Indian Dalit and anticolonial thought via Sartre's preface is traceable. The debate on whether political commitment endangers art runs through Progressive Writers vs. modernists in Indian literature.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Existence precedes essence: people make themselves and are free. Critique of Dialectical Reason adds individual praxis to Marxism. Groups-in-fusion and seriality describe how collective action forms. His politics: Communist partner to 1956, later Maoist sympathies, anti-colonial. Critics: Camus, Aron and moral critics attack his fellow-travelling. Debate questions Does radical freedom contradict historical materialism? Should intellectuals be political partisans?
Mao: Peasant Revolution and the Long March
A communist revolution without the proletariat

Mao Zedong's great innovation was to base a Marxist revolution on China's peasants. It brought him to power in 1949, but it also created a new type of party-army state. The route is the model for Maoist movements from Nepal to India's forests.
Collapse of the old order

The Qing dynasty fell in 1911. China split among warlords; the Nationalist (Kuomintang) Party under Chiang Kai-shek ran the Northern Expedition (1926-28). The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) was founded in 1921 with Soviet help. In April 1927, Chiang's Shanghai massacre crushed the urban communists. Mao (b. 1893 in Hunan) concluded that the revolution must rely on the countryside.
Report on Hunan (1927)

Mao's Report on an Investigation of the Peasant Movement in Hunan (1927) found that peasants were rising against landlords and called it a storm, "a tornado". The communists must lead, not hold back. "A revolution is not a dinner party." This contradicts Moscow's urban strategy, a break with Comintern advice.
Base areas and people's war

Mao and Zhu De built a Red Army in the Jinggang Mountains (1928), and later the Jiangxi Soviet (1931-34). Principles of guerrilla war: "the enemy advances, we retreat; the enemy camps, we harass; the enemy tires, we attack; the enemy retreats, we pursue". The army lives among the people "like fish in water". Land reform wins the peasants.
The Long March

Chiang's encirclement campaigns forced the Red Army out of Jiangxi in October 1934. About 86,000 started; some 6,000-8,000 and others joined later reached Shaanxi a year later, after marching about 9,000 km (figures vary). At the Zunyi conference (January 1935) Mao gained leadership. Yan'an became the base. The Long March became the founding myth of the party.
War with Japan and civil war

The Japanese invasion (1937) allowed the CCP to expand through nationalism and rural organisation: from about 40,000 in 1937 to over 1 million members by 1945. The Yan'an Rectification campaign (1942-44) imposed Mao's ideology and purged dissidents, a model for later campaigns. The civil war of 1946-49 ended with the PLA's victory, and Mao proclaimed the People's Republic on 1 October 1949.
Revolution and its price

Orthodox Marxists say a peasant revolution cannot be socialist; Trotskyists saw a bureaucratic deformity. Historians (Chalmers Johnson) credit nationalism and anti-Japanese resistance more than land reform; others (Mark Selden) credit social programmes. Land reform (1947-52) killed hundreds of thousands to over a million landlords, as the usual estimate, with some low and some high. Jung Chang and Jon Halliday ( Mao: The Unknown Story , 2005) are widely criticised for exaggeration. Defenders : it ended a century of humiliation and warlordism.
Maoist and Indian reception

Mao's China influenced the Indian left: Telangana (1946-51) imitated a peasant war, and in 1967 Naxalbari adapted Mao's base-area strategy (see lesson 4-2-1). The CPI(M)'s split in 1964 was partly pro-China sentiment. The 1962 border war confronted Indian communists with a loyalty question. Indian writers on the Long March, including Nehru and Edgar Snow's readers, admired it. The Nepal Maoist "People's War" (1996-2006) followed Mao and fed rebellion in India's "Red Corridor".
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Mao based revolution on the peasantry after the 1927 Shanghai defeat. Report on Hunan (1927) welcomed peasant rage. Guerrilla war and base areas; Long March (1934-35). Yan'an consolidated Mao's leadership; Rectification set the pattern of campaigns. Critics ask if it was nationalism or communism, and how much blood land reform cost. Debate questions Did Mao adapt Marxism or abandon it? Was the peasant road a model or a one-off?
Mao's Theory: Contradiction, Mass Line, New Democracy
Mao as thinker

Beyond the guerrilla and the leader, Mao wrote the texts that made "Maoism", sometimes "Mao Zedong Thought". They adapt Marxism-Leninism to a peasant land and became the programme of insurgents worldwide.

In caves at Yan'an, Mao studied and lectured. His essays On Practice and On Contradiction (1937), On Protracted War (1938), On New Democracy (1940), the Yan'an Talks on Literature and Art (1942) and On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People (1957) are the main texts. "Mao Zedong Thought" was written into the party constitution in 1945.
On Contradiction

Every thing contains contradictions; the principal contradiction and the principal aspect change with context. Under Japanese invasion, the contradiction with Japan was principal and the class struggle was secondary. He divides antagonistic from non-antagonistic contradictions. This became a flexible licence to change strategy. On Practice argues that knowledge comes from practice and returns to practice.
The mass line

"From the masses, to the masses": gather scattered ideas, concentrate them into policy, then test them with the masses. Cadres should go down and learn from peasants. It shapes Maoist ideas of participatory party work, though in practice the party decided.
New Democracy and the united front

In On New Democracy (1940) Mao argued that China, semi-colonial and semi-feudal, must first complete a bourgeois-democratic revolution, but under proletarian leadership, with a bloc of four classes: workers, peasants, petty bourgeoisie and the national bourgeoisie. After the revolution, an economy mixed under state leadership. This was meant to unify against imperialism and feudalism.
Application

New Democracy was the line from 1949 to about 1953; after that, collectivisation and nationalisation (1953-56) went faster. On the Correct Handling of Contradictions (1957) preceded the Hundred Flowers campaign (1956-57), when intellectuals were invited to criticise; when they did, the Anti-Rightist Campaign (1957-59) punished some 550,000 people. The theory justified both openness and repression depending on whether a contradiction was "among the people" or "with the enemy".
The elastic theory

Liberals say contradiction talk gives the leader a licence: whatever he declares principal is principal. Orthodox Marxists and Trotskyists see peasantism and nationalism. Althusser praised On Contradiction as an anti-Hegelian gem. Dissidents (Simon Leys) saw cynicism. Historians question whether the theory guided policy or justified decisions already taken. Maoist defenders insist the mass line differentiates it from Soviet bureaucratism.
Mao in Indian debates

The Maoist strand (CPI-ML, Naxalites, now CPI (Maoist), formed 2004) calls India semi-colonial and semi-feudal, which is the New Democracy analysis, and plans "New Democratic Revolution" and "protracted people's war". The CPI(M)'s Programme describes India as a capitalist-landlord state under a "People's Democratic" stage, also drawing on the stages idea. Debate over the "national bourgeoisie" divides left groups. Mass-line ideas influence the NGO and movement politics of Adivasi areas.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways On Contradiction: shifting principal contradictions give strategic flexibility. Mass line: from the masses, to the masses. New Democracy: four-class bloc under proletarian leadership. Contradictions "among the people" vs "with the enemy" justified both opening and repression. Maoism underpins armed movements in South Asia. Debate questions Is "principal contradiction" analysis a tool or an excuse? Does the mass line differ from top-down rule?
Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution
Two campaigns, the worst years of Maoism

Between 1958 and 1976 Mao launched two mass campaigns meant to speed up socialism and prevent its decay. One produced the largest famine in recorded history; the other tore apart the party, schools and society. Any serious judgement of communism must face them.
After the first Five-Year Plan

China's first Five-Year Plan (1953-57) used Soviet aid and a Soviet model. After 1956, Mao felt it was too slow and bureaucratic. He wanted mass mobilisation to overtake Britain in steel in 15 years. The Anti-Rightist Campaign (1957) silenced critics inside the party.
The Great Leap Forward (1958-62)

Peasants were gathered into huge people's communes with communal kitchens; backyard furnaces were meant to make steel; grain targets were raised. Officials, fearful, reported inflated harvests (some claims of several times the real output), so the state procured too much grain, left villages starving, and exported grain. Mao's campaigns on sparrows and deep ploughing damaged farms. At Lushan (1959) Marshal Peng Dehuai criticised the Leap and was purged.
The famine

Death estimates vary: official Chinese-era demography suggests about 15-30 million excess deaths; Yang Jisheng ( Tombstone , 2008) counts about 36 million; Frank Dikötter ( Mao's Great Famine , 2010) about 45 million, including up to 2.5 million beaten or tortured to death; some demographers (Cao Shuji) reach 32 million or more. Most estimates fall between about 15 and 50 million; around 30 million is the most often cited figure. Mao removed from day-to-day running of the state by 1962, Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping restored private plots.
The Cultural Revolution (1966-76)

Mao feared that Soviet-style revisionism and bureaucracy were creeping back, and that "capitalist roaders" like Liu Shaoqi sat in the party. In May 1966 he launched the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution: students formed Red Guards , attacked teachers, "old" culture and officials. Liu was persecuted and died in custody in 1969. Armed factional fights broke out in 1967-68; the army restored order; millions of youths were "sent down" to the countryside. The Gang of Four (including Jiang Qing) were arrested in October 1976.
Toll and verdict

Deaths in the Cultural Revolution are estimated from about 0.5 to 2 million (some sources go higher); tens of millions suffered persecution. Education collapsed, universities closed until 1977-78, and cultural heritage was destroyed. In 1981, the Party's Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party judged the Cultural Revolution a disaster and held that Mao made "gross mistakes" but remained "70% good, 30% bad" (an often-quoted formula attributed to Deng).
Competing readings

Liberals and historians (Dikötter, Roderick MacFarquhar) stress Mao's responsibility and the system's lack of feedback: no press or opposition to report famine. Amartya Sen cited the Leap to show that democracy prevents famine. New Left sympathisers (Maurice Meisner, Alain Badiou) see the Cultural Revolution as a genuine attempt to fight bureaucracy and equality, though it failed. Sceptical Marxists note its use as a purge. Chinese nationalists now accept the "Mao era" while limiting discussion: the topic remains restricted in China.
China's lessons in India

India's own planners avoided collectivisation after seeing both China and the USSR. Sen's comparison of India and China ( Hunger and Public Action , 1989 with Drèze) argues that India's democracy prevented famine after 1947, while China's growth since 1978 outpaced India's. The Naxalites (1967) idealised the Cultural Revolution, praising the "Chinese path", and the slogan "China's Chairman is our Chairman". Today Indian Maoists have dropped none of the claim; others see the Leap as a warning against forced change.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Great Leap Forward (1958-62): communes, backyard steel, inflated reports. Famine of 1959-61: 15 to 55 million deaths depending on source, with 30-45 million commonly cited. Cultural Revolution (1966-76): Red Guards, purges, economic and educational damage; 0.5-2 million deaths. 1981 Resolution condemned the Cultural Revolution. Debate: famine as policy failure of a system lacking feedback or of one man. Debate questions Do these cases prove that one-party systems lack feedback? Can any social goal justify the Cultural Revolution?
Deng Xiaoping and Socialism with Chinese Characteristics
A communist party that embraced markets

Since 1978 China's economy has grown at about 9% a year for decades, lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty under a communist party. Is it socialism, state capitalism, or something new? The answer shapes what we think "communism" means in the 21st century.
After Mao

Mao died on 9 September 1976; the Gang of Four fell. Deng Xiaoping, twice purged (1966 and 1976), emerged as leader by December 1978 (Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee). "It doesn't matter whether a cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice" is his famous line (1960s, in Sichuan dialect).
Reform and opening

From 1978: dismantle the communes (household responsibility system, 1979-83), allow township and village enterprises, set up Special Economic Zones (Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Shantou, Xiamen), attract foreign investment, then reform state firms from 1990s. Deng's slogan "seek truth from facts" replaced class-struggle priority. The "Four Modernisations" were agriculture, industry, defence, science and technology.
Four Cardinal Principles and "socialist market economy"

Deng held that reform needed political stability: keep the Four Cardinal Principles (socialist road, people's democratic dictatorship, Party leadership, Marxism-Leninism-Mao Zedong Thought). In his 1992 Southern Tour he argued that markets are not unique to capitalism. The 14th Party Congress (1992) adopted the "socialist market economy". Later leaders added Jiang Zemin's "Three Represents" (2000-02) allowing private entrepreneurs into the Party.
Results and costs

Per capita GDP rose fantastically: extreme poverty (World Bank measure) fell from about 88% of the population in 1981 to near zero by 2020, by official claims. China became the "world's factory". But inequality rose sharply (Gini about 0.47 by many estimates), with environmental damage, corruption, and hukou-based discrimination against migrant workers. Tiananmen: the army crushed the protests on 3-4 June 1989; estimates of the dead range from several hundred to several thousand.
Xi Jinping era

Under Xi Jinping (leader since 2012) the Party has re-centralised, with the end of presidential term limits in 2018, a "common prosperity" drive (2021) and renewed tech-sector and property regulation, plus mass surveillance and the Xinjiang camps (hundreds of thousands to over a million Uyghurs detained according to UN and independent estimates, which China denies). In October 2022 Xi began a third term as General Secretary. A reader should check the latest data for developments after 2025.
Is it socialism?

Liberals : authoritarian capitalism with no political freedom; no "socialism". Chinese leaders : the primary stage of socialism will last a century. Marxist critics (David Harvey in A Brief History of Neoliberalism , 2005; Ho-fung Hung; Au Loong-yu) see a neoliberal process with Chinese traits. Pro-China left (Giovanni Arrighi, Adam Smith in Beijing , 2007): a market economy under state control, an alternative path. Workers' rights groups document strikes (thousands yearly) and suppression of independent unions.
India and China compared

India liberalised in 1991, 13 years after China; China's per capita GDP overtook India's and is now about five times larger. India's communists, in particular the CPI(M), have watched China's model with interest and in West Bengal (2006-11) tried Special Economic Zones, with disaster at Nandigram (March 2007: 14 killed in police firing). The 1962 war and the 2020 Galwan clash (20 Indian soldiers killed) strain ties. Debate: can democratic India copy an export-led, state-led model?
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Deng's reforms from 1978 ended communes and opened to markets and trade. Four Cardinal Principles keep Party control; "socialist market economy" (1992) is the formula. Rapid growth and poverty reduction; rising inequality and repression. Tiananmen (June 1989) shows the limit of reform. Disputes: socialism, state capitalism or neo-authoritarian growth. Debate questions Can a one-party state sustain markets indefinitely? Is China a socialist success story or a cautionary one?
Ho Chi Minh and Vietnam
Communism fused with nationalism

Vietnam shows the strongest case for communism as a vehicle of national liberation. Ho Chi Minh defeated France and, after him, the United States. It also shows the costs: war deaths in the millions, re-education camps and a one-party state still in power.
French Indochina

France conquered Vietnam in the 19th century and ruled it as part of Indochina until 1954. Ho (born Nguyen Sinh Cung, 1890) left in 1911 as a ship's cook, lived in Paris, joined the French Communist Party at the Tours Congress in 1920, studied in Moscow, and founded the Indochinese Communist Party in 1930. He proclaimed independence on 2 September 1945.
National liberation first

In Paris Ho reported on colonialism and wrote Le Procès de la colonisation française (1925). After reading Lenin's "Theses on the National and Colonial Questions" (1920), he said it was this that made him a communist: it promised liberation for his people. The Viet Minh (1941) united all patriots under a nationalist banner, with land reform and anti-Japanese resistance. Marxism was an instrument of independence.
People's war

General Vo Nguyen Giap built the army. The Viet Minh defeated the French at Dien Bien Phu (May 1954); at Geneva Vietnam was divided at the 17th parallel, with elections promised for 1956 but never held. In the North, Ho's government carried out land reform (1953-56) in which thousands were executed (estimates range from several thousand to tens of thousands) and the leadership later apologised for errors.
The second war

South Vietnam under Ngo Dinh Diem was backed by the US. The National Liberation Front (Viet Cong) rose in 1960. Direct US intervention began in 1965 (after the Gulf of Tonkin incident, 1964). Ho died on 2 September 1969. The Tet Offensive (1968) shook American opinion; the Paris Accords (January 1973) led to US withdrawal. Saigon fell on 30 April 1975. Total Vietnamese deaths in the wars 1955-75 are commonly estimated at 1.5 to 3.5 million, and some 58,000 Americans died.
After unification

Reunified Vietnam (1976) imposed collectivisation in the South, sent hundreds of thousands to "re-education" camps, and had about 800,000 or more "boat people" escape. Its 1978 invasion of Cambodia ended the Khmer Rouge; China attacked in 1979. Facing shortages, the Party launched Doi Moi (renovation) in 1986: markets, private firms and foreign investment, with Party control. Vietnam's GDP has grown 6-7% a year; it is now a manufacturing hub.
Hero or hardliner?

Admirers (Frances FitzGerald, Ho's own anti-colonial record) see a patriot. Critics : executions and land-reform terror; the ban on opposition; the repression of dissidents (e.g. the Nhan Van-Giai Pham affair, 1956-58); and the "re-education" camps. Historians (Fredrik Logevall, Embers of War , 2012) note missed chances for compromise in 1946-47. Realists : the US misread a nationalist movement as a Soviet proxy and fought a war it could not win. Marxists doubt that Doi Moi is socialism.
Solidarity with Vietnam

India recognised the Democratic Republic only in 1972, but Nehru and the Left had backed Vietnam's independence; India chaired the International Control Commission after 1954. The slogan "Hanoi, Saigon" marches of the 1960s and the CPI(M)'s activism show a deep solidarity. Today India and Vietnam have a "Comprehensive Strategic Partnership" (2016), partly around the South China Sea. Vietnam's Doi Moi is studied in India's debates on a reform path while preserving the state's role.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Ho became a communist through Lenin's anti-colonial theses. The Viet Minh united nationalists; Dien Bien Phu (1954) ended French rule in the north. The American war (1965-73) ended with the fall of Saigon (1975). Post-1975: re-education camps, boat people, then Doi Moi (1986). Debate: nationalist hero or Leninist autocrat. Debate questions Was Vietnam's communism more nationalism than Marxism? Does Doi Moi mean the end of socialism?
Castro and the Cuban Revolution
A revolution ninety miles from the USA

Cuba's 1959 revolution created a communist state in the Western Hemisphere that has survived more than six decades under US embargo. It inspired much of Latin America's left and also produced a long record of repression.
Batista's Cuba

Cuba was formally independent from 1902 but dominated by the US (the Platt Amendment, 1901-34). Fulgencio Batista seized power in 1952. Inequality was sharp: Havana was rich, rural areas poor. Fidel Castro (born 1926), a lawyer, led an attack on the Moncada barracks on 26 July 1953, was jailed ("History Will Absolve Me"), and exiled in Mexico, where he met Che Guevara.
Guerrilla victory

Castro landed with 82 men on the yacht Granma in December 1956; survivors formed a guerrilla group in the Sierra Maestra. Urban sabotage and peasant support, plus Batista's unpopularity and an arms embargo, led to the regime's collapse. Batista fled on 1 January 1959. At first the 26 July Movement was not formally communist and Castro promised elections.
Turn to socialism

Agrarian Reform (1959) took land; US firms were nationalised in 1960 after oil-refining disputes; the US imposed an embargo (1960-62) and backed the Bay of Pigs invasion (April 1961). Castro declared the revolution socialist, and in December 1961 declared himself a Marxist-Leninist. The Cuban Communist Party formed (1965) and the 1976 constitution set a one-party state. Soviet subsidies made up a large part of the economy.
Social gains and costs

Literacy campaign (1961): near-universal literacy; a healthy-life record: infant mortality fell to about 4-5 per 1,000 (official), life expectancy about 78; many doctors, exported abroad. But: political prisoners (thousands in the 1960s), the UMAP labour camps for dissidents and homosexuals (1965-68), no free press, emigration (over a million by the 2020s), and rationing. Estimates of executions in 1959-60s vary from hundreds to several thousand.
The Special Period and beyond

Soviet collapse in 1991 cut GDP by roughly a third: blackouts, hunger and "balsero" emigration (1994). Tourism, remittances and Venezuelan oil (from 1999) helped. Fidel handed power to Raul in 2006-08; Obama's opening (2014-16) was partly reversed by Trump. Protests on 11 July 2021 were the largest in decades, followed by arrests. Economic reforms (2011 and later) allow small private businesses. In 2024-25 Cuba suffered blackouts and shortages; check current data.
The two Cubas

Supporters : sovereignty against US pressure; high health and education standards; the embargo (judged illegal by almost all UN General Assembly votes yearly) hurts. Critics : Human Rights Watch and Amnesty document repression of dissent; the economy stagnates; wages are tiny. Economists : Cuba's indicators come at a high price in efficiency and freedom. Historians (Louis Pérez) emphasise US dominance before 1959. Marxists debate whether Cuba is a workers' state or a bureaucratic state-capitalism.
Cuba and India

India supported Cuba at the UN and in the Non-Aligned Movement. Fidel Castro visited India for the 1983 NAM summit in New Delhi, where he handed the chair to Indira Gandhi with a famous hug, and again in 1973 for a short trip. Cuban doctors and vaccines found markets in India; India's CPI(M)-led Kerala often cited Cuba as an example of health and education achievements on low income. The Kerala model is compared to Cuba in development studies.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Castro's guerrillas toppled Batista on 1 January 1959. Radicalisation under US hostility led to socialism, 1961, and Soviet ties. Gains in literacy and health; costs in repression and stagnation. 1991 ended Soviet aid; reforms are limited. Debate: sovereignty under siege versus a failed economy and dictatorship. Debate questions How much of Cuba's problems are due to the US embargo and how much to its system? Are health and education gains worth the loss of political freedom?
Che Guevara and the Foco Theory
The icon and the strategy

Che's face is on millions of T-shirts. His strategy of small guerrilla bands creating the conditions for revolution (foco) was tried across Latin America, mostly with failure. The gap between icon and record is the lesson.
From doctor to revolutionary

Ernesto "Che" Guevara (b. 1928, Rosario, Argentina) trained as a doctor and travelled through Latin America ( The Motorcycle Diaries , written 1952, published 1993). He saw the 1954 US-backed coup in Guatemala. He joined Castro in Mexico, fought in the Sierra Maestra, and led the capture of Santa Clara (December 1958). In Cuba, he headed the La Cabaña prison tribunals (executions, 1959), the National Bank, and the Industry Ministry.
Foco theory

In Guerrilla Warfare (1960), Che claimed that (1) popular forces can win against an army; (2) one need not wait for all conditions of revolution to exist, since the insurrection creates them; (3) the countryside is the arena. Régis Debray ( Revolution in the Revolution? , 1967) systematised "foquismo": a small armed vanguard in rural areas acts first; the party follows. It reversed Lenin's order, which put the party first.
The New Man

In "Man and Socialism in Cuba" (1965) he argued for moral over material incentives and the formation of a "new man" through voluntary labour. As industry minister (1961-65) he sought rapid industrialisation without market incentives, with poor results; sugar was neglected. He also criticised the Soviet Union for its "manual of capitalism" in 1965.
Internationalism

Che called for "two, three, many Vietnams" (1967 message to the Tricontinental). He went to the Congo (1965) to help Laurent Kabila's rebels and left after failure. In 1966 he moved to Bolivia, where the Communist Party refused support and peasants did not join; the army, aided by the CIA, captured him. He was executed on 9 October 1967 in La Higuera.
Foco failed nearly everywhere

Guerrilla movements in Venezuela (1960s), Peru, Colombia (the ELN), Guatemala, and Argentina (Montoneros, ERP) were defeated, often leading to harsh military regimes (Argentina's junta, 1976-83). Exceptions: Nicaragua's Sandinistas (1979), which joined many classes, and FMLN's stalemate in El Salvador. Cuba itself was not a pure foco: the urban underground, middle-class opposition and Batista's collapse were crucial.
Hero or killer?

Admirers : Che's sacrifice and sincerity; anti-imperialism. Critics : he oversaw executions without fair trials in 1959 (estimates from 55 to more than 150 at La Cabaña) and supported labour camps; he praised hatred. Latin American communists said foco bypassed organising. Sartre called him "the most complete human being of our age". Historians (Jon Lee Anderson, 1997) are mixed. Liberals point to contrasts: Che's economic failures and his youth cult. Defenders : he fought for the poor.
Che in India

The Naxalite movement (1967-) was partly influenced by Che and Mao: Charu Majumdar stressed armed struggle by small squads, a foco-like approach, criticised by the CPI(M) as "adventurism". Che visited India in 1959 (July), meeting Nehru in Delhi, and wrote of his impressions in letters. His image remains a youth icon in Kerala and Bengal. The debate "party first or armed action first" divides Indian Maoists.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Che's Guerrilla Warfare (1960) and Debray developed foco: armed vanguard creates conditions. Moral incentives and "new man" ideas guided his economics. Failure in Congo and Bolivia; death on 9 October 1967. Foco failed across Latin America, with harsh reprisals. Critics note La Cabaña executions; admirers his sacrifice. Debate questions Can armed action substitute for patient political organisation? How should we weigh Che's ideals against his record?
Cambodia and the Khmer Rouge
The most extreme case

The Khmer Rouge ruled Cambodia from 1975 to 1979 and, in under four years, killed or caused the deaths of an estimated quarter of the population. It forces the question of how a communist movement could produce a genocide, and whether the ideology or local conditions are to blame.
War spreads to Cambodia

Prince Sihanouk's neutral Cambodia was drawn into the Vietnam War: US bombing (1969-73, over 500,000 tons by many estimates) and the coup of Lon Nol (1970) fuelled a civil war. The Khmer Rouge, led by Pol Pot (Saloth Sar), trained in Paris and a member of the Communist Party, grew from a small force to winners. They took Phnom Penh on 17 April 1975.
Year Zero ideology

The Khmer Rouge aimed at an agrarian utopia: abolish money, markets, religion, private life and cities; to "reset" society in "Year Zero". Cities were emptied within days (2 million in Phnom Penh), people forced into rural collectives, and Angkar ("the Organisation") controlled all. Pol Pot pushed rice targets of three tons per hectare. Influences: Maoism and the Great Leap, French radical thought, Khmer nationalism, and a deep suspicion of urban "new people" (the "base people" were privileged).
Terror and Tuol Sleng

At least 1.5 to 2 million died from execution, forced labour, starvation and disease, about a fifth to a quarter of the 7-8 million people. Educated people, Buddhist monks, Cham Muslims and ethnic Vietnamese were targeted; the party also purged itself. At the Tuol Sleng (S-21) prison, about 14,000-20,000 were tortured and killed; only a handful survived. The "killing fields" such as Choeung Ek are now memorials.
Overthrow and survival

Border clashes led Vietnam to invade in December 1978; Phnom Penh fell on 7 January 1979. Vietnam installed a government under Heng Samrin. China, Thailand and the US backed the Khmer Rouge's retention of the UN seat for years. Pol Pot died in 1998 without trial. The Khmer Rouge Tribunal (ECCC, 2006-2022) convicted Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan of genocide and crimes against humanity (2018) and Kaing Guek Eav ("Duch") of crimes.
Explaining Cambodia

Scholars offer: US bombing and civil war radicalised the movement (William Shawcross); an ideology merging Maoist agrarianism with Khmer chauvinism (Ben Kiernan, who stresses race and genocide); a Leninist party, secret and paranoid, with total power (David Chandler); Cold War politics, with Chinese support. No single cause is accepted; each contributes. The Vietnamese invasion and the 1991 Paris Accords led to the UN mission (1992-93) and elections.
Communism or aberration?

Anti-communists ( The Black Book of Communism , 1997) treat Cambodia as the logical end of the ideology. Left critics : it was a perversion with nationalist and racist elements; Marx supposed that socialism arises from an industrial working class, not agrarian "Year Zero". Realists : it shows how an unchecked party, armed by war, can do anything. Chomsky and Herman drew criticism in 1977-79 for doubting early reports. Historians agree that the regime killed on a massive scale; the number is disputed (about 1.5 to 2 million; demographers' range 1.2 to 2.8 million), and "genocide" applies to ethnic groups.
Reactions in India

India's official line was complex: the Janata government (1977-79) condemned Khmer Rouge violence; in 1980 the Indira Gandhi government recognised the Heng Samrin regime in Phnom Penh, one of the few non-communist states to do so, which many saw as supporting Vietnam. The Indian left was embarrassed; the CPI(M) condemned Pol Pot's regime. Indian writers use Cambodia in debates on ultra-left adventurism, such as the Naxalite critique and the question of party violence.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways The Khmer Rouge governed from April 1975 to January 1979. Emptying the cities, forced collectives, abolition of money and religion. About 1.5-2 million died; Tuol Sleng; targeted groups. Vietnam's invasion ended the regime; UN tribunal verdict 2018. Debate: logic of communism, or a unique deviation? Debate questions Does Cambodia indict Marxism or Leninist party rule or neither? Why did the world tolerate the Khmer Rouge's UN seat?
African Socialism: Nyerere, Nkrumah, Sankara
Socialism after empire

After 1957 African states became independent in a world divided between capitalism and communism. Many leaders called their path "African socialism". Some followed Marx, others rejected class struggle as foreign. The results, from Tanzania to Burkina Faso, are instructive.
Decolonisation

Ghana became independent in 1957, and 17 African states in 1960. Leaders such as Nkrumah, Nyerere, Touré (Guinea), Keita (Mali) and Senghor (Senegal) rejected Western capitalism as colonial, and looked to planning, state ownership and one-party unity. The Cold War offered Soviet and Chinese aid.
Nyerere and Ujamaa

Julius Nyerere , Tanzania's president (1961-85), proposed ujamaa (familyhood), based on traditional African communal life. The Arusha Declaration (1967) nationalised banks and big firms and set a leadership code limiting officials' wealth. From 1973-76 about 80% of rural Tanzanians were moved into ujamaa villages, often by force. Output fell, and Tanzania stagnated and needed food imports.
Nkrumah and pan-Africanism

Kwame Nkrumah (Ghana, 1957-66) wrote Consciencism (1964) and Neo-Colonialism, the Last Stage of Imperialism (1965), adapting Lenin: formal independence masks continued economic domination. He built the Volta dam and promoted a United States of Africa. His rule became authoritarian (Preventive Detention Act 1958, one-party state 1964), and a coup in 1966 overthrew him.
Sankara's "Africa's Che"

Thomas Sankara took power in Upper Volta in 1983 and renamed it Burkina Faso (1984). He launched mass vaccination (2.5 million children in 15 days), a literacy drive, tree planting, bans on female genital cutting and forced marriage, and austerity for officials. He refused IMF loans. Some forced measures and the dissolution of unions angered groups. He was assassinated on 15 October 1987 in a coup led by Blaise Compaoré, who ruled until 2014.
Results

Most African socialist experiments ended in coups, debt, or turned to the IMF in the 1980s structural adjustment era. Tanzania, though poor, avoided civil war and built national unity and a common Swahili language. Mozambique (FRELIMO, Machel) and Angola (MPLA) adopted Marxism-Leninism, and endured long civil wars (Angola 1975-2002; Mozambique 1977-92) with Cold War proxies. Ethiopia's Derg (1974-91) killed hundreds of thousands, including in the Red Terror, and the 1983-85 famine.
Why it failed

Liberals : state control and one-party rule created rent-seeking and dictatorship. Marxists : African "socialism" ignored class and was a nationalist ideology of new elites (Issa Shivji, Samir Amin). Economists : weak states and commodity dependence limited planning. Historians point to Cold War meddling (Lumumba killed 1961; Nkrumah's 1966 coup with Western approval) and debt. Defenders : Nyerere's moral vision and egalitarianism have lasted in Tanzanian politics.
Afro-Asian solidarity

Nehru and the Bandung Conference (1955) set up Afro-Asian solidarity; Non-Aligned Movement (1961). Indian planners and Gandhians influenced Nyerere; Nyerere admired Gandhi. India's technical cooperation (ITEC) and trade with Tanzania stem from this. The Indian diaspora in East Africa faced Uganda's expulsion of Asians (1972, Idi Amin), a reminder of the limits of solidarity. Sankara is a popular icon among Indian youth movements.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways African socialism rejected capitalism but often rejected class struggle. Nyerere's ujamaa: nationalisation and forced villagisation; Tanzania poor but stable. Nkrumah: neo-colonialism and pan-Africanism; authoritarian drift. Sankara: reforms and austerity, assassinated 1987. Marxist-Leninist states in Angola, Mozambique, Ethiopia suffered war and famine. Debate questions Was African socialism socialism or nationalism? Did external intervention or internal choices doom these experiments?
Liberation Theology and Allende's Chile
Two Latin American experiments

In 1970 Chile elected a Marxist president, Salvador Allende, hoping for a democratic road to socialism. In 1973 he was overthrown by a coup. Around the same time Latin American priests were fusing Christianity and Marxist social analysis. Both test whether socialism can be reached by peaceful and faith-based means.
Latin America in the 1960s

Inequality, land concentration and military rule were widespread. Cuba's example and the Alliance for Progress (1961) vied for attention. The Second Vatican Council (1962-65) and the Medellín Conference of Latin American bishops (1968) declared a "preferential option for the poor".
Liberation theology

Gustavo Gutiérrez, a Peruvian priest, wrote A Theology of Liberation (1971): salvation includes liberation from poverty and oppression. Leonardo Boff (Brazil), Jon Sobrino and Oscar Romero (assassinated 24 March 1980 in El Salvador) took up the cause. Base communities studied the Bible for justice. It used Marxist ideas (class analysis, structural sin) though not materialist philosophy. The Vatican (Cardinal Ratzinger, 1984 and 1986 instructions) criticised its Marxist borrowing, and Boff was silenced in 1985.
Allende's "Chilean road"

Allende led the Popular Unity coalition (socialists, communists, radicals), and won 36.6% in 1970, a plurality; Congress confirmed him. His policy: nationalise copper (unanimous vote of Congress, 1971), banks and big estates, raise wages, redistribute land, "socialism with red wine and empanadas". Growth in 1971 was strong; then inflation (over 300% by 1973), shortages and strikes (truckers' strike, 1972 and 1973) followed. The US (Nixon, Kissinger; CIA) funded opposition and tried to block him.
The coup and the dictatorship

On 11 September 1973 General Augusto Pinochet led a coup; La Moneda was bombed and Allende died (the official finding: suicide). The regime killed about 3,200 people and tortured tens of thousands (Rettig and Valech commissions: roughly 3,200 dead or disappeared and about 40,000 victims of torture or detention). Chicago-trained economists ("Chicago Boys") introduced neoliberal policy, with growth later but high inequality. A 1988 plebiscite ended Pinochet rule; democracy returned in 1990.
Legacies

The coup was cited by many on the left (including Berlinguer's "historic compromise" in Italy, 1973) as proof that bourgeois democracy cannot be used by socialists; others stress that Allende lacked a majority and a unified coalition. Liberation theology shaped base communities, the Sandinistas (priests in government in Nicaragua), and Brazil's Landless Workers' Movement (MST). From the 1990s its influence waned as Pentecostal churches and Vatican policy grew; Pope Francis (2013-2025) reopened a friendlier relation.
Judging both

Conservatives : Allende's policies were ruinous and violated the law. Left critics : the Chilean left under-armed and split (MIR vs. Communists). Liberals : Allende was a democrat but his coalition included revolutionary rhetoric. Historians assign the US a part, but the main cause was Chilean elite and military action. Marxists (Poulantzas, Mandel) debate the lesson. Theologians : liberation theology risks reducing faith to politics (Ratzinger); defenders see it as true Gospel.
Faith and revolution in India

Indian Christian theologians such as Samuel Rayan, and Dalit theologians such as A.P. Nirmal, adapted liberation theology to Indian caste and poverty. The Jesuit priest Stan Swamy, working with Adivasis in Jharkhand, died in custody in July 2021 after his arrest in the Bhima Koregaon case. Gandhi's own mix of faith and politics, and Ambedkar's Buddhism as social liberation, offer parallels. Kerala's experience of an elected communist government (1957) invited Chile-like comparisons: Kerala's was dismissed by the Centre under Article 356 in 1959.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Liberation theology (Gutiérrez, 1971) makes the poor central to Christian faith. Allende (1970-73) tried a democratic road to socialism. Economic crisis, polarisation and US pressure preceded the 11 September 1973 coup. The Pinochet regime killed about 3,000 and tortured tens of thousands. Debate: can socialism come through elections? Debate questions What does Chile teach about democracy and revolution? Is liberation theology faith or politics?
Communism in India: M.N. Roy to the CPI(M)
The largest communist movement in a democracy

India has had the world's most successful electoral communism: governments in Kerala, West Bengal and Tripura for decades. It also shows splits, errors, and decline, and offers evidence on whether Marxism can work in a poor, caste-divided democracy.
Origins

Roy (1887-1954), a Bengali revolutionary, took part in the Second Comintern Congress (1920), proposing "Supplementary Theses" against Lenin's view of colonial bourgeoisie. The Communist Party of India's origin is dated 1920 (Tashkent) by some and 1925 (Kanpur) by the party. S.A. Dange, Muzaffar Ahmad and Singaravelar organised unions. The British brought the Peshawar (1922-23), Kanpur (1924) and Meerut (1929-33) conspiracy cases.
Strategy and debates

Roy argued that India's bourgeoisie would compromise with imperialism, so workers must lead. Dange and Ranadive (the "Ranadive line", 1948-50) called for insurrection and branded Nehru a puppet; this failed. The party later chose the parliamentary road. The "Andhra Thesis" (1950) preferred a Mao-style peasant war. Programmatically, the CPI backed a "National Democratic" stage; the CPI(M) a "People's Democratic" one.
Telangana, Kerala, Bengal

In Telangana (1946-51) communists led peasants against the Nizam and landlords; about 3,000 villages were liberated and land was redistributed. In Kerala, E.M.S. Namboodiripad's ministry (April 1957) passed land and education reforms and was dismissed in 1959. In West Bengal, the Left Front (1977-2011) under Jyoti Basu carried out Operation Barga (tenant registration, about 1.5 million sharecroppers) and decentralised panchayats.
Splits and decline

The party split in 1964 into the CPI (pro-Moscow, support for Congress) and the CPI(M) (the "Left"). The Naxalite split followed in 1967-69. In 2011 the Left Front lost power in West Bengal after 34 years, after Singur and Nandigram (2006-07) disputes; in 2018 it lost Tripura. In 2014 and 2019 Lok Sabha elections the left won fewer than 10 seats; in 2024 about 8. Kerala (LDF, since 2016) remains the main stronghold; the 2021 victory broke its alternation. Results of the 2026 state elections are not covered here.
What the Left achieved

Kerala achieved high literacy, health indicators and low fertility, with land reform and public action; the "Kerala model" is cited in development studies. West Bengal's land reform raised rural security. But industrial growth lagged; West Bengal saw capital flight and "party-society" control, and killings during elections. Fraternal parties argue they defend secularism: the CPI(M) was a main opponent of communal politics.
Why the decline?

Liberals : ideology and union militancy discouraged investment; one-party control in Bengal. Dalit critics (Ambedkarites): leadership was upper-caste (mostly Brahmin, Kayastha and Nair), caste ignored. Radical Marxists : the Left became parliamentarist and managed capitalism. Feminists : little women's leadership. Historians : split over the 1962 war and Sino-Soviet issue, and misjudged 1942, "Quit India", reducing nationalist standing. Defenders : Left pressure kept Indian politics welfarist.
Reading the Indian left

This whole lesson is Indian, so consider the key debate: class versus caste. Ambedkar said that caste, not class, is India's division; E.M.S. wrote The National Question in Kerala (1952) and "Marx-Gandhi" essays; B.T. Ranadive and Basavapunnaiah led the CPI(M). Intellectual strands include D.D. Kosambi, Irfan Habib, K.N. Panikkar and Prabhat Patnaik. Recent Left politics link with caste-justice (Dalit and Bahujan groups) and with student movements (JNU).
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Roy and the CPI (1920-25) formed the Indian left amid British repression. Strategies swung from insurrection (1948-50) to the parliamentary road. Success in Kerala, West Bengal and Tripura; decline since 2011. 1964 split into CPI and CPI(M); Naxalites split in 1967. Critiques: caste blindness, upper-caste leadership and industrial failure. Debate questions Why has the Indian left not become a national force? Is class politics enough in a caste society?
Naxalbari, Charu Majumdar and Maoism in India
India's longest internal war

The Maoist insurgency, which the Indian government once called the "single biggest internal security challenge" (Manmohan Singh, 2006), began in a Bengal village in 1967. It reveals unresolved questions of land, forests, tribal rights and the state.
Naxalbari, 1967

In the Naxalbari area of Darjeeling district, West Bengal, tenant farmers led by CPI(M) radicals (Kanu Sanyal, Jangal Santhal) seized land in March-May 1967. On 25 May a police firing killed 11 (mostly women and children). The United Front government (including CPI(M)) then suppressed the uprising. Radicals left the party and formed the All-India Coordination Committee of Communist Revolutionaries (1967).
Charu Majumdar's Historic Eight Documents

Charu Majumdar (1918-72) wrote the "Historic Eight Documents" (1965-67) and in 1969 founded the CPI(ML). His line: India is semi-colonial, semi-feudal; the Chinese path of agrarian revolution and "annihilation of class enemies" (landlords) by small squads, "Chairman Mao is our Chairman", election boycott, and rejection of mass organisations as revisionist. Violence became the central tool.
Rise, repression and fragmentation

Naxalism spread to Bihar, Andhra, Srikakulam, and urban Calcutta, where students attacked "class enemies" and statues. The state responded with brutal police action, including "encounters", and in 1971 Operation Steeplechase (army). Majumdar was arrested in July 1972 and died in Lalbazar lockup on 28 July. The movement split into dozens of groups. A key successor: the CPI(ML) Liberation (electoral), and the People's War Group (Andhra, 1980) and Maoist Communist Centre (Bihar).
The CPI (Maoist) and the Red Corridor

In September 2004 the PWG and MCC merged into the CPI (Maoist). It operated in a "Red Corridor" from Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand through Odisha and Andhra, mostly in forested Adivasi districts rich in minerals. Violence peaked in 2010: the Dantewada ambush killed 76 CRPF men (April 2010). Salwa Judum (2005-11), a state-backed militia, was ruled illegal by the Supreme Court in Nandini Sundar v. State of Chhattisgarh (2011).
Decline and the state's campaign

Violence deaths (civilians, security forces and insurgents) fell from about 1,000 a year around 2010 to a few hundred in the late 2010s, and districts affected fell from about 180 to fewer than 50 by 2024 per government data. The government set March 2026 as the target to end Left-wing extremism. As of 2025, security forces reported killing the CPI (Maoist) general secretary Basavaraju (May 2025); on 30 March 2026, the Home Minister told Parliament that India was free of Naxal violence, ahead of the 31 March deadline; critics say the root causes in tribal areas remain.
Grievance and method

Sympathisers (Arundhati Roy, Nandini Sundar) stress displacement, forest rights violations, and state violence on Adivasis. Government and critics : Maoists extort, kill villagers as "informers", destroy schools and recruit children; they obstruct development. Marxists (CPI(M)) call it adventurism. Researchers (Alpa Shah, Nightmarch ) show a mix of idealism and coercion. Courts criticise both sides. The Forest Rights Act (2006) and the PESA (1996) address some grievances but implementation is weak.
This is the Indian angle

The Naxal question is tied to the Fifth and Sixth Schedules of the Constitution (tribal areas), land reform failures, mining (Niyamgiri, Odisha), displacement and policing. Government policy mixes security operations with development schemes (the "SAMADHAN" doctrine, 2017, and aspirational districts). Writers like Mahasweta Devi ( Hajar Churashir Maa , 1974) and filmmakers show the early idealism. Debates continue on talks, surrender policies, and the human cost.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Naxalbari (1967) began a peasant uprising; the CPI(ML) was founded in 1969. Charu Majumdar stressed annihilation of class enemies and Mao's path.
