Fragmentation after 1972; CPI (Maoist) formed 2004 and spread in the Red Corridor. Peak violence around 2010; steady decline since. Debate: grievance and rights versus insurgent violence. Debate questions Is armed struggle ever justified in a democracy? What would resolve the underlying Adivasi grievances?
Eurocommunism and the New Left
Communism with a democratic face

After 1956 and 1968 many Western communists and radicals sought a socialism that was neither Soviet nor social democratic. Eurocommunism (1970s) and the New Left raised questions still alive: can a revolutionary party accept pluralism, and can radicals change society without a vanguard?
Two shocks

The Secret Speech and Hungary (1956) drove many from Communist parties. The Soviet crushing of the Prague Spring (August 1968) deepened the break. The same year, student revolts in Paris (May 1968), the US and Germany questioned all authority. The New Left appeared: E.P. Thompson, Ralph Miliband, C. Wright Mills (who coined "New Left" in 1960).
The New Left

It stressed agency, culture, democracy and personal freedom. It drew on Gramsci, Sartre, Marcuse and the humanist Marx. New Left Review (1960, Perry Anderson from 1962) and the Students for a Democratic Society's Port Huron Statement (1962) expressed it. The issues: war (Vietnam), race (civil rights), gender, ecology. Its concerns were less about industrial workers.
Eurocommunism

The Italian (PCI, Enrico Berlinguer), French (PCF, Georges Marchais) and Spanish (PCE, Santiago Carrillo) parties in the 1970s accepted parliamentary democracy, pluralism, and independence from Moscow. Carrillo's Eurocommunism and the State (1977) criticised the Soviet model. Berlinguer's "historic compromise" (1973) proposed an alliance with the Christian Democrats after Chile. In 1976 the PCI won 34% in Italy, its peak.
Theory: the road to socialism

Eurocommunists drew on Gramsci's war of position, Poulantzas's State, Power, Socialism (1978) and on Togliatti's "Italian road". They dropped the "dictatorship of the proletariat" (the French party in 1976). The goal: a democratic transition within a mixed economy and a plural society, with a new relationship between party and movements. Other currents (Trotskyists, Maoists) rejected this as reformism.
Results

Eurocommunists never held national power in Western Europe (the Italian PCI supported but didn't join governments in 1976-79; the PCF joined Mitterrand's government in 1981-84). After 1979 (Thatcher), 1980s (Soviet crisis) and the changing working class, the parties declined; the PCI dissolved in 1991 and became the Democratic Party of the Left. Spain's PCE shrank. The New Left's legacy lives in new social movements, the Greens and cultural politics.
From left and right

Moscow called it anti-Soviet. Orthodox and Trotskyist critics : it is social democracy in a red coat and gave up revolution. Liberals doubted the commitment to pluralism, noting that internal party democracy was weak. Conservatives : communist parties had a record of supporting Soviet policy (the PCF supported the USSR on Afghanistan in 1980). New Left critics : the movement neglected organisation and fragmented into identity politics. Defenders : it kept democratic socialism alive in Southern Europe.
The Indian New Left

The CPI(M)'s decision to work within parliamentary democracy and form state governments resembles Eurocommunism, though it rejects the label. Indian New Left currents, such as the 1970s student movements (Navnirman in Gujarat, 1974; JP Movement), the feminist and Dalit Panthers (1972) and environmental movements (Chipko, 1973), reflect a post-1968 mood. The Emergency (1975-77) shaped a similar democratic turn among communists, as the CPI's support of the Emergency split the left.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways The 1956-68 shocks produced the New Left and Eurocommunism. Eurocommunists accepted pluralism and independence from Moscow. Berlinguer's historic compromise (1973) followed Chile. Peak: PCI 34% in 1976; decline after 1980. Critics: reformism, tied to Soviet record, and weak organisation. Debate questions Can a communist party fully accept pluralism? Was Eurocommunism a transition to social democracy?
Dependency and World-Systems: Frank, Amin, Wallerstein
Why are poor countries poor?

Modernisation theory said poor countries were simply behind and would follow the rich. Dependency and world-systems theorists said they were poor because of how they were tied to the rich. The debate shaped development policy, UN politics and India's economic thinking.
Latin American roots

In 1949 Raúl Prebisch (UN Economic Commission for Latin America) argued that primary exports lose value relative to manufactures, so poor countries stagnate: the Prebisch-Singer hypothesis. After the Cuban Revolution, Marxists (Frank, dos Santos, Amin, Rodney) made the argument radical. Lenin's Imperialism was one ancestor.
Frank: development of underdevelopment

Andre Gunder Frank ( Capitalism and Underdevelopment in Latin America , 1967) argued that Latin America's underdevelopment was created by its integration into the world capitalist market since the 16th century: metropolis-satellite chains drain surplus. Recommendation: delink or revolution. Critics note his model resembled circulation rather than production.
Amin, Rodney, Cardoso

Samir Amin ( Accumulation on a World Scale , 1970; Unequal Development , 1973) analysed "unequal exchange" and calls for "delinking". Walter Rodney ( How Europe Underdeveloped Africa , 1972) traced Africa's poverty to slavery and colonialism. Fernando Henrique Cardoso and Enzo Faletto ( Dependency and Development in Latin America , 1969) gave a milder view: "associated-dependent development" can occur. Cardoso later became Brazil's president (1995-2003).
Wallerstein: the modern world-system

Immanuel Wallerstein ( The Modern World-System , vol. 1, 1974) described a single capitalist world economy since the long 16th century, with a core , semi-periphery and periphery and cycles of hegemony (Dutch, British, American). The semi-periphery (e.g. Brazil, India, Russia) stabilises the system. Giovanni Arrighi traced cycles of finance. Wallerstein saw the system in terminal crisis.
East Asia and Latin America

Empirically, the case is mixed. The East Asian "tigers" (South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore) and later China climbed to wealth by integrating with the world market under state guidance, which dependency theory said was impossible. In Latin America, import substitution (1950s-70s) yielded growth and then debt crises (1982). Africa's stagnation 1980-2000 supports some claims. Recent growth in Africa and India complicates the story.
Evidence and logic

Neoclassical economists (Bhagwati, Balassa) point to the success of export-led growth in East Asia. Marxists (Robert Brenner, Bill Warren, Imperialism: Pioneer of Capitalism , 1980) argue that capitalism does develop the periphery, and that Frank follows trade not production relations. Historians (Cooper) say the world-system blurs differences. Post-colonial critics: Eurocentric categories. Defenders : persistent core-periphery gaps and commodity dependence support a basic insight (Prebisch).
Drain and self-reliance

India's thinkers anticipated dependency: Naoroji's drain, R.C. Dutt, and the Nehru-era planners' import substitution and self-reliance. India's closed economy (1950s-80s) reflected a mild delinking. Marxist economists Utsa and Prabhat Patnaik ( A Theory of Imperialism , 2016) and Amiya Bagchi ( Private Investment in India , 1972) continue the tradition; Amin influenced the Indian left. After 1991 India became a semi-periphery success story and an example for both sides.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Dependency theory: underdevelopment results from ties to the core. Frank, Amin, Rodney: delinking and unequal exchange; Cardoso: dependent development. Wallerstein: core, semi-periphery, periphery in a capitalist world system. East Asian growth challenged the thesis; commodity dependence supports it. India's drain theory is an early form of the argument. Debate questions Does East Asia refute dependency theory? Is India now core, periphery or semi-periphery?
Analytical Marxism and G.A. Cohen
Marxism with analytic rigour

In the late 1970s a group of philosophers and economists decided to state Marx's claims in clear language, test them with tools from economics and logic, and keep only what survived. The result, "Analytical Marxism", is the most academic, and one of the most honest, forms of the tradition.
The September Group

Starting in 1979, a group (the "No-Bullshit Marxism group") met in London: G.A. Cohen, Jon Elster, John Roemer, Erik Olin Wright, Adam Przeworski, Philippe Van Parijs, Robert Brenner and others. Cohen's Karl Marx's Theory of History: A Defence (1978) is their founding text. They used rational choice, game theory and neoclassical economics.
Cohen on history

Cohen reconstructed historical materialism: the productive forces tend to develop, and relations of production exist because they promote that development (the development thesis and a functional explanation ). Relations become fetters, and are replaced. He relied on a technological reading. Critics asked how functional explanation works without a mechanism.
Roemer on exploitation

John Roemer ( A General Theory of Exploitation and Class , 1982) showed that exploitation can be defined using unequal ownership of assets, without the labour theory of value; in game-theoretic models, classes emerge from market exchange. His later work proposed "market socialism" with coupons. Wright's Classes (1985) and Envisioning Real Utopias (2010) mapped class structure and ways to expand democratic economic power.
Cohen on justice and equality

Later Cohen turned to political philosophy: Self-Ownership, Freedom, and Equality (1995) attacked Nozick's libertarianism; If You're an Egalitarian, How Come You're So Rich? (2000) and Why Not Socialism? (2009) argued that socialist ideals of community and equality have moral force and a camping-trip example shows people cooperating without markets. He admitted that problems of incentive and information remain, and doubted that large-scale socialism is feasible.
Influence and decline of the group

The group's members spread across universities; by 1990s most dropped the label. Elster abandoned Marxism; Przeworski studied democracy and found democratic social democracy superior to revolution; Wright built a major empirical class project. Practical influence: basic income debates (Van Parijs, Real Freedom for All , 1995), stakeholder-society ideas and the Rawlsian-Marxist dialogue.
Is it Marxism?

Orthodox and dialectical Marxists (Ellen Meiksins Wood, Harry Cleaver) say it strips the dialectic, class struggle and revolutionary praxis, leaving "Marxism without Marx". Economists find the models too simple. Philosophers : functional explanation needs a causal mechanism (Elster). Political critics : no strategy for change. Defenders : clarity exposes weak arguments; it saved the best parts of Marx for academic debate. Liberals welcome that it takes justice seriously.
Analytic ideas in India

Analytical Marxism's tools influenced Indian economists studying agrarian class: Pranab Bardhan's work on land, labour and rural poverty ( Land, Labor and Rural Poverty , 1984) used rational-choice models and bargaining. Roemer's market socialism connects with debates on state and market in India after 1991. Amartya Sen's work on capabilities (not a Marxist school, but dialogues with it) shares the concern for equality. Indian debates on reservations and basic income (Economic Survey 2016-17) show applied justice debates.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Analytical Marxists restated Marx in analytic style. Cohen defended a technological, functional theory of history. Roemer defined exploitation without the labour theory of value. Cohen later defended socialist equality, admitting limits. Critics: lacks the dialectic and strategy. Debate questions Is Marxism without the labour theory still Marxism? Can justice arguments substitute for revolutionary politics?
Post-Marxism: Laclau, Mouffe and Žižek
After the working class

If the industrial proletariat is not the agent of history, what is? Post-Marxists keep a left politics but drop class as the centre. Their ideas run through modern populism, identity politics and radical democracy.
After 1968 and 1989

New social movements (feminism, ecology, anti-racism, gay rights) did not fit class politics. French post-structuralism (Foucault, Derrida, Lacan) challenged fixed essences. The collapse of 1989 ended the credibility of the Soviet model. Ernesto Laclau (Argentine) and Chantal Mouffe (Belgian) wrote Hegemony and Socialist Strategy (1985).
Laclau and Mouffe: no necessary class

Hegemony and Socialist Strategy (1985) argues that identities are built in discourse, not fixed by economic position. Society has no ultimate foundation; groups form chains of equivalence against a common adversary. Political success depends on hegemonic articulation, not on economic laws. Marxism's "last instance" never arrives. Their goal: radical and plural democracy .
Populism and agonism

Laclau's On Populist Reason (2005) argues that populism, building a "people" against "elites" by linking demands, is a form of politics, not a pathology. Mouffe ( For a Left Populism , 2018; Agonistics , 2013) argues that politics needs adversaries, not enemies: conflict channelled democratically. They influenced Podemos in Spain and Syriza's and Corbyn's strategies.
Žižek: ideology and the Real

Slavoj Žižek (b. 1949, Slovenia) fuses Lacanian psychoanalysis, Hegel and Marx: The Sublime Object of Ideology (1989). Ideology works by enjoyment and by what we do, not what we say ("they know very well, but still they do it"). He defends Lenin and "revolutionary terror" provocatively ( Revolution at the Gates , 2002), criticises liberal multiculturalism, and writes on film. His Living in the End Times (2010) lists four horsemen of crisis.
Politics of the post-Marxists

Podemos (2014) used Laclau's thought; Syriza won power in Greece in 2015 and then accepted austerity; Corbyn's Labour surged in 2017 and lost in 2019. Right-wing populism (Trump, Orbán, Modi's Hindutva populism by some readings) uses similar techniques, an irony noted by critics. Žižek has commented on every crisis, with controversial remarks.
From Marxists and others

Norman Geras (1987, "Post-Marxism?") argued they abandoned materialism: without economic structure, there is no reason for a left. Ellen Meiksins Wood ( Retreat from Class , 1986) accused them of "true socialism". Liberals welcome pluralism but see populism as risky. Žižek's critics accuse him of flippancy, and apology for violence. Feminists and race theorists say identity is material. Defenders : a necessary revision after class politics failed to capture many movements.
Hegemony, populism and India

Laclau's populism is used to analyse Indian politics: the AAP (2012) in Delhi, Indira Gandhi's "Garibi Hatao" (1971) and the BJP's Hindutva with development. Partha Chatterjee's The Politics of the Governed (2004) uses "political society", close to post-Marxist ideas. The Subaltern Studies group moved from Marxism to post-structuralism in the 1990s. Identity-based movements, Dalit, Bahujan and women's, illustrate the "chain of equivalence" idea. Critics argue class is still key in India.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Laclau and Mouffe (1985): identities are built politically, not given by class. Radical democracy and chains of equivalence. Populism as a political logic; agonism as healthy conflict. Žižek blends Lacan, Hegel and Marx and defends Lenin provocatively. Critics: abandon materialism, class, and risk populism. Debate questions Is populism a left or a right strategy? Can class politics be replaced by discourse?
Marxist Feminism and Social Reproduction
Whose work counts?

Marx analysed wage labour but wrote little on housework, childcare and care. Marxist feminists asked: who produces the workers? Their answer, social reproduction, linked the family to capitalism and still shapes debates on unpaid work and gender.
Engels and after

Engels's Origin of the Family (1884) tied women's subordination to private property; August Bebel's Woman and Socialism (1879) and Clara Zetkin built socialist women's movements (International Women's Day, 1910-11 proposals). Alexandra Kollontai in Russia pushed for communal childcare. In the 1970s, second-wave feminism revived the question.
The domestic labour debate

In the 1970s Margaret Benston, Mariarosa Dalla Costa and Selma James ( The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community , 1972) argued that housework produces labour power and is unpaid labour that capital relies on. They launched Wages for Housework . Others asked whether housework produces value in Marx's sense.
Social reproduction theory

Lise Vogel ( Marxism and the Oppression of Women , 1983) and later Tithi Bhattacharya ( Social Reproduction Theory , 2017) say capitalism depends on the unpaid and paid labour that sustains workers and raises the next generation: childcare, cooking, schooling, health. Women's oppression arises from the relation between production and reproduction. Capital resists paying for care, and treats it as free; crises in care come when the state cuts services.
Dual systems and intersectionality

Dual systems theorists (Heidi Hartmann, "The Unhappy Marriage of Marxism and Feminism", 1979) argue that patriarchy is a separate system interlocking with capitalism. Intersectional thinkers (Angela Davis, Women, Race and Class , 1981; the Combahee River Collective, 1977; Kimberlé Crenshaw coined the term in 1989) show that race and class shape women's experience. Silvia Federici ( Caliban and the Witch , 2004) links witch-hunts to primitive accumulation and the disciplining of women's bodies.
Women under communism

The USSR legalised abortion (1920), easy divorce and women's suffrage, and mobilised women into industry and medicine. But the 1930s reversed it: abortion banned 1936-55, "Mother Heroine" awards. The "double burden" of wage work plus housework persisted. Women made up 30-40% of the workforce in China, with Mao's "women hold up half the sky", yet little in top political roles. In Eastern Europe, women's labour force participation was high, with weak change in the household division of labour.
Questions and objections

Orthodox Marxists say housework is not value-producing; class remains primary. Radical feminists say patriarchy predates capitalism; Marxism subordinates gender to class. Liberal feminists pursue equal rights, not systemic change. Economists say household production is hard to price (Wages for Housework wasn't adopted). Historians : socialist states had records mixed with gains and failures. Defenders : the theory explains why care crises recur.
Gender, caste and care

Indian Marxist feminists (Maria Mies on the lace-makers of Narsapur, The Lace Makers of Narsapur , 1982; Vina Mazumdar; Leela Gulati; Uma Chakravarti) show how housework, home-based labour and caste combine. Indian women's movements of the 1970s (Shramik Sangathan, SEWA founded 1972 by Ela Bhatt, anti-dowry and Mathura rape case protests, 1979-80) are part of the story. The labour-force participation of Indian women (about 37% in 2022-23 by PLFS, up from 23% in 2017-18) and unpaid care work (time-use survey 2019: women spend about 4-5 hours a day on unpaid domestic work) raise the questions Marxist feminists posed. Ambedkar added caste patriarchy.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Marx neglected domestic work; Marxist feminists put it at the centre. Social reproduction theory: capitalism relies on unpaid care that produces labour power. Dual systems and intersectional theories widen the analysis. Socialist states gave women rights and jobs but kept the double burden. Critics argue about value, priorities, and class versus patriarchy. Debate questions Should unpaid care work be paid or valued by the state? Is patriarchy a separate system or part of capitalism?
Eco-Socialism and Degrowth
Capitalism meets climate

If capitalism needs endless growth and the planet is finite, is the system in conflict with the biosphere? Eco-socialists say yes and look to Marx. Critics reply that the Soviet Union and Maoist China were environmental disasters. The question is central to climate politics.
Marx on nature

Marx wrote of the "metabolic rift" between town and country: Liebig's finding that soil nutrients shipped to cities weren't returned ( Capital Vol 3). John Bellamy Foster ( Marx's Ecology , 2000) argues Marx had an ecological side; Ted Benton and Daniel Tanuro disagree. The Marx of the Manifesto also praised capitalism's mastery of nature, which "Promethean" critics point to.
Eco-socialism

Joel Kovel ( The Enemy of Nature , 2002), Michael Löwy, James O'Connor ("second contradiction of capitalism": it undermines its own natural conditions) and Jason W. Moore ( Capitalism in the Web of Life , 2015, "Capitalocene") argue that capitalism, not "humanity" in general, drives ecological crisis. The remedy: democratic planning of production, public ownership of energy, shorter work, and a green transition.
Degrowth

Associated with Serge Latouche, Giorgos Kallis ( Degrowth , 2018), and Jason Hickel ( Less Is More , 2020), degrowth proposes scaling down material throughput in rich countries while improving wellbeing: shorter hours, universal services, caps. Hickel cites studies that "green growth" cannot decouple resource use from GDP absolutely at the needed speed. Not all eco-socialists accept it; some favour "green new deal" growth.
Soviet and Chinese records

State socialism was ecologically poor: the draining of the Aral Sea (cotton irrigation, since the 1960s), Chernobyl (1986), Norilsk and Magnitogorsk pollution, Mao's "man must conquer nature" campaigns (the Four Pests campaign, 1958, killed sparrows and hurt crops; the Leap's deforestation). Eastern European countries emitted heavily per unit of GDP. These cases show lack of accountability, not a lack of planning.
Politics today

Green New Deal proposals (US 2019, Europe 2019) mix public investment and decarbonisation. Calls for "climate justice" connect to Indigenous movements (e.g. Standing Rock). Bolivia's Pachamama law (2010) and Cochabamba summit (2010), Ecuador's Yasuní proposal, and Kerala's people's planning show attempts. Meanwhile, China is both the largest emitter (about 30% of global CO2) and the largest installer of solar and wind.
Challenges

Liberal environmental economists (Nordhaus) favour carbon taxes and markets; evidence shows capitalist states have cut emissions too (the UK, EU) while growing. Free-market environmentalists say property rights protect nature. Developing countries object that degrowth harms the poor; the "right to development". Marxist critics of degrowth (Kohei Saito's degrowth communism, Capital in the Anthropocene , 2020, is a counterexample) argue about growth. Historians : state socialism polluted horribly, so planning isn't sufficient.
Gandhi, Chipko and the environmentalism of the poor

Ramachandra Guha and Madhav Gadgil describe India's "environmentalism of the poor": Chipko (1973), the Narmada Bachao Andolan (1985), and forest-rights struggles. Gandhi's "the earth provides enough to satisfy every man's need but not every man's greed" is often quoted. Kerala's Silent Valley campaign (1970s-84) saved a forest. The CPI(M) supported growth and dams in West Bengal. India's per-capita emissions are far below the global average (about 2 tonnes CO2 in 2022 vs. about 4.7 global), so equity matters in negotiations; its 2070 net-zero pledge (announced 2021) is contested.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Marx's "metabolic rift" gives the Marxist ecological starting point. Eco-socialists see capitalism's growth imperative as the root of crisis. Degrowth advocates reducing material use in rich countries. The Soviet and Maoist record was ecologically terrible. Debate: green growth versus degrowth; developing countries' needs. Debate questions Can capitalism decouple growth from emissions? Should rich countries degrow while poor ones grow?
The Economic Critique: Mises, Hayek and the Calculation Problem
The strongest argument against planning

The most powerful academic case against socialism is not moral but practical: without market prices, no planner can know what to produce. Whether it is decisive remains a central debate between economists, and a test for every Marxist claim about planning.
Vienna, 1920

After the Bolshevik Revolution and War Communism, Ludwig von Mises, an Austrian economist, wrote "Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth" (1920) and the book Socialism (1922). He argued that socialism, by abolishing private ownership of the means of production, abolishes the market prices which allow rational allocation. In 1936 Oskar Lange answered; Friedrich Hayek and others pressed the debate through the 1930s-40s.
Mises: prices and calculation

Complex economies require choices among millions of possible uses of resources. Prices that arise in free exchange of private property show relative scarcity and allow profit-and-loss accounting. Without markets for capital goods, planners cannot compare costs. Mises: "Where there is no free market, there is no pricing mechanism; without a pricing mechanism, there is no economic calculation." (paraphrase). The result is chaos, not planning.
Hayek: knowledge

In "The Use of Knowledge in Society" (1945) Hayek reframed the problem: relevant knowledge is dispersed, local and often tacit. Prices are a signal system that coordinates millions of people without anybody needing to know the whole. The Road to Serfdom (1944) added the political claim that central planning leads to coercion. Hayek also criticised "constructivist rationalism".
The reply: Lange, Lerner, Taylor

Oskar Lange (1936-37) proposed market socialism : a Central Planning Board sets prices by trial and error (like Walras's auctioneer), managers follow rules, and firms are state-owned. Abba Lerner added marginal-cost rules. Lange said socialism could calculate, and in fact could do better than capitalism on externalities and income distribution. Hayek replied that it ignored knowledge and incentives. Kornai ( The Socialist System , 1992) described the "soft budget constraint".
The record and the computer age

Soviet planning built industry, but failed to match capitalist consumer goods and innovation. Planners used "material balances" and bargaining; shadow prices emerged in black markets. Yugoslavia's self-management and Hungary's "goulash" reform tried markets. Today, supporters of planning (Cockshott and Cottrell, Towards a New Socialism , 1993; Leigh Phillips and Michal Rozworski, The People's Republic of Walmart , 2019) argue that computers and big data make planning feasible; Amazon and Walmart plan internally at scale.
Of the critique

Market socialists (Lange, Roemer): you can have prices without private capital. Marxists (Nove, The Economics of Feasible Socialism , 1983) accept the calculation problem partly but stress negotiated coordination. Keynesians : markets are also unstable and produce unemployment and inequality, not true efficiency. Behavioural economists : even market prices ignore externalities such as carbon. Austrian critics : computing power doesn't solve tacit knowledge or incentives. Historians : Mises's 1920 argument arrived before the Soviet experience, and was later vindicated in part.
Planning in India

India's planning from 1951 (the Planning Commission, abolished 2014 and replaced by NITI Aayog) was an experiment in democratic planning with a mixed economy. Critics of the licence-permit raj (B.R. Shenoy's dissent note, 1955; Jagdish Bhagwati and T.N. Srinivasan; Bhagwati-Desai, 1970) used arguments close to Hayek's about information and incentives. P.C. Mahalanobis's model assumed planners could pick priorities; Sukhamoy Chakravarty defended planning. The 1991 reforms abandoned most licensing. Debate persists around price controls, MSP and public sector firms.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Mises (1920): no private property in capital means no market prices and no rational calculation. Hayek (1945): prices aggregate dispersed knowledge. Lange: market socialism with a planning board; Kornai: soft budget constraint. Soviet record supports part of the critique; big-data planning is a contested rebuttal. India's licence-permit raj illustrates the planning debate. Debate questions Can computers solve the knowledge problem? Does the calculation argument also apply to large corporations?
The Liberal Critique: Popper, Berlin, Arendt
Rights versus utopia

Liberal critics accept that capitalism has faults but argue that Marxism's historical laws and utopian goals endanger freedom. Their arguments, from the 1940s to the 1950s, shaped the Cold War mind and still frame modern liberalism.
Fugitives from totalitarianism

Karl Popper (Vienna to New Zealand), Isaiah Berlin (born in Riga, Oxford) and Hannah Arendt (Germany to the US) all fled Nazism and had Soviet communism in view. They wrote in the 1940s-60s, in a time of fear of atomic war and "total" ideologies.
Popper: the open society

In The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945), Popper attacked Plato, Hegel and Marx as "historicists" claiming laws of history. Such theories are unfalsifiable: Marxism, he said, resisted refutation by redefining its claims. He backed "piecemeal social engineering" (small reforms that can be corrected) against "utopian engineering". The criterion for good politics: you can remove bad governments without violence. The Poverty of Historicism (1957) continued.
Berlin: two concepts of liberty

In "Two Concepts of Liberty" (1958), Berlin distinguished negative liberty (freedom from interference) from positive liberty (self-mastery, becoming one's "true" self). The danger: a state that claims to know your true interests can force you to be free, as in Jacobin and communist regimes. He defended value pluralism : human goods conflict and cannot be perfectly harmonised, so a final solution is an illusion. In "Historical Inevitability" (1954) he attacked determinism.
Arendt: totalitarianism

The Origins of Totalitarianism (1951) treated Nazism and Stalinism as a new form of rule based on ideology, terror, and the camps, grounded in atomised, lonely masses. It differs from tyranny, since it aims to remake human nature. The book's claim of a symmetry between the two regimes is debated. In The Human Condition (1958) she praised political action, and in On Revolution (1963) she argued that the American Revolution founded freedom, but the French led to the social question dominating politics.
Cold War liberalism

These ideas fed into the Congress for Cultural Freedom (1950-67, covertly funded by the CIA), anti-communism, and "end of ideology" theses (Daniel Bell, 1960). After 1989, they were cited by Eastern European dissidents. Fukuyama's "end of history" (1989, 1992) echoed it. They also were used to justify anti-communist crackdowns such as McCarthyism, which Arendt and Berlin deplored.
Of the critics

Marxists (Marcuse, Perry Anderson): Popper misreads Marx, who did not claim inevitable laws; liberalism ignores structural unfreedom (e.g. economic dependence). Philosophers of science (Kuhn, Lakatos): falsification is too simple. Charles Taylor and republicans: negative liberty is too thin. Historians : the totalitarian model ignored internal diversity (revisionists such as Fitzpatrick) and colonial violence by liberal states (Césaire's "Discourse on Colonialism", 1950). Feminists : Arendt neglected gender. Defenders : the 20th century proved their warnings.
Liberty in India

Berlin's negative liberty informs debates on Article 19 rights and on free speech and the right to privacy ( Puttaswamy , 2017). Positive liberty is used to defend welfare rights under Directive Principles and the right to education. Ambedkar's Constituent Assembly speech (25 November 1949) distinguished political from social and economic democracy and warned of "hero-worship", in a spirit close to liberal-constitutional caution. Indian liberals such as Minoo Masani (Swatantra Party, 1959) and Jayaprakash Narayan's evolution from Marxism to democratic socialism are parallels.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Popper: historicism is unscientific; prefer piecemeal reform and open criticism. Berlin: guard negative liberty, beware positive liberty, accept pluralism. Arendt: totalitarianism is a new form of rule based on terror and ideology. Cold War liberalism shaped anti-communist thinking after 1945. Critics: strawman of Marx, colonial blind spots, thin liberty. Debate questions Is value pluralism compatible with any egalitarian programme? Did Popper fairly describe Marx?
Totalitarianism, Famines and the Human Cost
The ledger

Any honest study of communism must face the death toll: tens of millions from famine, terror, camps and war. The numbers are disputed; so is what they show. This lesson sets out the ranges historians give, and how to read them.
Counting the dead

Opening Soviet archives in 1991 gave new data, trimming some earlier estimates (such as Conquest's tens of millions for Stalin's terror) but leaving the magnitude huge. The Black Book of Communism (Courtois et al., 1997) gave a widely cited total of about 100 million; its contributors disagreed with the figure (Werth and Margolin gave lower numbers), and scholars say it includes deaths from famine and wars. Rudolph Rummel's higher figures (over 100 million) are viewed as inflated.
Soviet Union

Estimates for deaths from policies, 1917-53, run from about 6-9 million (lower, "documented") to 15-20 million; with civil-war deaths added, higher. Famine 1932-33 about 5.5-8.7 million. Great Terror 1937-38: about 680,000 executions. Gulag: 1.5-1.7 million died in camps and colonies (1930-53). Deportations killed several hundred thousand. Timothy Snyder ( Bloodlands , 2010) counted about 14 million in the territories between Germany and Russia in 1933-45 (both regimes).
China, Cambodia and others

China: the famine 1959-61 (15-55 million; central 30-45 million); land reform 1947-52 (hundreds of thousands to over 1 million); Cultural Revolution (0.5-2 million). Cambodia: 1.5-2 million. North Korea: famine of the 1990s (about 600,000 to 1 million by various estimates), and camps. Ethiopia's Derg: perhaps 500,000 in the Red Terror and famine; Vietnam, Laos and Eastern Europe: tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands. A broad estimate: 60-100 million for all communist regimes, depending on definitions.
Totalitarianism and its debate

Arendt, Friedrich and Brzezinski (1956) used "totalitarianism" for a model with one party, ideology, secret police and monopoly of media and arms. Revisionists argue regimes were more chaotic and negotiated, with local initiative (Fitzpatrick, Getty). The "intentionalist vs structuralist" split is also found in studies of Nazi Germany. Another debate: whether famine was policy (Ukraine), neglect (China's Leap) or deliberate.
Comparisons and context

Comparisons with capitalism: critics note colonial famines (Bengal 1943; the Irish famine of the 1840s; Congo Free State, 1885-1908, estimated 1-10 million deaths) and wars. Communists reply that the Black Book counts famines but not British colonial ones. Historians answer that the comparison doesn't excuse; the key distinction is that these deaths were caused by a regime that claimed to be building a better world, and that the world should hold both to account. Also, communist regimes lowered mortality through health programmes in some respects (Cuba, Kerala, China's early gains in life expectancy).
Of the ledger and of apologies

Anti-communists : the deaths flow from the ideology (no checks, class "enemies"). Left defenders : ordinary economic stress, war, and imperialism contributed; counting is politicised (Domenico Losurdo, Stalin: History and Critique of a Black Legend , 2008, is widely criticised). Historians (Snyder, Applebaum, Getty, Davies): seek careful ranges, caution about both denial and inflation. Amartya Sen : absence of free press and elections explains the scale of famines. Moral philosophers : do consequences alone define the verdict, or does intent?
India and famine

India experienced the Bengal famine of 1943 (2-3 million dead; Amartya Sen's analysis: food availability decline was small, entitlements collapsed), and no major famine since 1947, which Sen credits to democracy and a free press. Indian communists were slow to acknowledge Stalin's crimes until 1956, and Chinese famine data were hardly known. Ambedkar's essay "Buddha or Karl Marx" (1956) rejected violence as a means to Marxist ends. Kerala and West Bengal's communists argued for non-violent, parliamentary paths. Maoist violence in India today revives the question.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Estimates of deaths under communist regimes range roughly from 60 to 100 million, with big uncertainties. USSR: famine, terror, Gulag; China: 15-55 million in the famine; Cambodia: 1.5-2 million. Opening archives cut some figures but confirmed the scale. "Totalitarian" model versus revisionist accounts. Debate on ideology, comparison, and the role of free press (Sen). Debate questions Do the numbers settle the question of communism? How should one compare famine deaths under colonial, capitalist and communist rule?
The Dissidents: Djilas, Solzhenitsyn, Havel
Critics from inside

The most telling critiques of communism came from people who lived under it. They did not just count deaths: they described a system of lies, privilege and fear, and showed how citizens could resist. Their ideas, "living in truth", helped topple regimes in 1989.
Dissent after Stalin

After 1956 and the Thaw, writers and intellectuals in the Soviet bloc began to speak out: samizdat (self-published typescripts), tamizdat (published abroad), underground seminars, and protest groups such as Charter 77 in Czechoslovakia and the Helsinki Groups in the USSR after the 1975 Helsinki Accords.
Djilas: the new class

Milovan Djilas, once Tito's deputy, wrote The New Class (1957) while in prison: communism created a new ruling class of party bureaucrats who own the means of production by controlling them, with privileges and no accountability. The classless society was a myth. He was jailed for nine years in all. Trotsky had said something similar, but Djilas's inside account was explosive.
Solzhenitsyn: the Gulag

Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn (1918-2008), a decorated artillery officer who spent 8 years in camps and in exile, published One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich (1962). The Gulag Archipelago (published in Paris, 1973-75) documented the camp system based on testimonies of 227 witnesses; the KGB seized a copy and he was arrested and expelled in February 1974. His Harvard speech (1978) criticised the West also. His call: "live not by lies".
Havel: the power of the powerless

Václav Havel (1936-2011), playwright, wrote the essay The Power of the Powerless (1978). His example: a greengrocer who puts a sign "Workers of the world, unite!" in the window not from belief but from fear and habit. The regime is held up by everyone's small compliances. When one person "lives in truth", refusing the ritual, the façade cracks. After Charter 77, he was jailed (1979-83) and in December 1989 became president of Czechoslovakia. Others: Sakharov (physicist, Nobel Peace Prize 1975), Sharansky, Kołakowski, Adam Michnik ( A New Evolutionism , 1976).

Polish Solidarity (1980) joined workers and intellectuals; the Round Table talks (1989) led to partly free elections on 4 June 1989. In Czechoslovakia, the Velvet Revolution (17 November-29 December 1989). Dissidents became ministers and presidents (Havel, Walesa, Michnik as editor). Soviet dissidents suffered psychiatric prisons and labour camps; Sakharov was exiled to Gorky (1980-86) and freed by Gorbachev.
Limits of dissent

Pro-regime voices : dissidents were unrepresentative and Western-funded. Historians (Timothy Garton Ash, Kotkin): dissent mattered mainly by keeping a moral alternative alive and by the regime's loss of faith, not by mass movements. Solzhenitsyn's own record : Russian nationalist and critics note his anti-Western illiberalism, his reported antisemitic tropes in Two Hundred Years Together (2001-02). Left critics : dissent after 1989 was converted into neoliberal reform. Radicals : some wanted democratic socialism, not capitalism (Michnik, Kuroń, Kołakowski initially).
Dissent in India

Indian analogues of dissidents appear in the Emergency (1975-77): Jayaprakash Narayan, Morarji Desai and thousands detained (MISA) while the CPI backed Indira Gandhi and the CPI(M) opposed. George Fernandes' resistance and the underground press recall samizdat. Indian public intellectuals read Solzhenitsyn and Havel, and the Left's debates about "internal" versus "external" criticism run on. Ambedkar's and Gandhi's moral politics (satyagraha, "truth-force") mirror "living in truth".
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Djilas: communism produced a new class of party bureaucrats. Solzhenitsyn exposed the Gulag as a system; expelled in 1974. Havel: ordinary compliance sustains regimes; "living in truth" breaks it. Dissent helped prepare 1989 through Charter 77 and Solidarity. Critics note nationalist and illiberal streaks and limits of influence. Debate questions Does the greengrocer example hold for democracies too? Can moral resistance topple a regime without material crisis?
Communist States Today: China, Vietnam, Cuba, Laos, North Korea
Communism still governs about a fifth of humanity

Five states are still ruled by communist parties: China, Vietnam, Cuba, Laos and North Korea (the last officially Juche, no longer "communist" in its constitution since 2009-12 wording). They run very different economies. As of 2025, their record shows what the label means in practice.
Survivors of 1989-91

After 1989-91 these regimes survived by different paths. China and Vietnam turned to markets while keeping Party rule; Laos followed; Cuba and North Korea kept more of the command economy. All keep one-party systems, state control of media, and strong security services. Combined, they hold about 1.5 billion people, mostly in China.
China

Under Xi Jinping (leader since 2012), the Party emphasises "Xi Jinping Thought", anti-corruption, tech self-reliance and "common prosperity". GDP per capita is about USD 13,000 (2023 nominal); the economy is second-largest. Problems: a property-sector crisis since 2021, youth unemployment, demographic decline (population falling since 2022), and repression in Xinjiang, Tibet and Hong Kong (National Security Law, 2020). The 21st Party Congress is due in 2027.
Vietnam and Laos

Vietnam grew at 6-7% a year and became an export hub; its Party (General Secretary Nguyen Phu Trong died in July 2024, and To Lam succeeded him) tolerates little dissent and has anti-corruption "blazing furnace" purges. Laos, a small landlocked state, rules through the Lao People's Revolutionary Party (since 1975), with heavy debt to China (the China-Laos railway, 2021) and an economic crisis (high inflation and debt distress since 2022).
Cuba and North Korea

Cuba suffers blackouts, a shortage of food and fuel, and an exodus (over a million left in 2021-24 by some estimates). It allowed small private firms (2021 law on MSMEs), yet a monetary reform in 2021 triggered inflation. North Korea (Kim Jong Un since 2011) is a hereditary state with nuclear weapons (tests 2006-2017), a famine in the 1990s (the "Arduous March", 600,000-1 million dead by some estimates), and the world's most closed society; UN inquiry (2014) found crimes against humanity. Deepened ties with Russia since 2023 (troop deployment 2024) are reported.
What do they share?

Features: Party leadership clause in the constitution; mass organisations; control of press and the internet (China's Great Firewall); a state security apparatus; and commemorations of founders. Divergences: in China and Vietnam, performance legitimacy (growth) and nationalism; in Cuba, anti-imperialism and social services; in North Korea, personality cult and military. The theory is a legitimising language rather than a guide to policy, many scholars say.
Are these communist?

Marxists : these are state capitalisms or bureaucratic states, not communism (Marx foresaw a stateless society). Party apologists : socialism in the "primary stage" will take generations (the CCP's "1 to 100 years" phrasing). Liberals : authoritarian developmental states using Leninist organisation. Human rights groups (Amnesty, HRW, Freedom House: all five are rated "Not Free") document restrictions on speech, assembly and religion. Comparative economists : success of China and Vietnam supports state-led, market-oriented growth, not communism as such.
India and its communist neighbours

China is India's largest neighbour, trade partner (bilateral trade over USD 100 billion) and rival: the 1962 war, the Doklam standoff (2017), and the Galwan clash (2020). Relations eased after the October 2024 patrolling agreement; verify later developments. India-Vietnam ties are strategic (Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, 2016). India has long-standing ties with Cuba (medical aid, vaccines). The Indian Left's views differ: the CPI(M) holds that China is building socialism with Chinese characteristics.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Five states are ruled by communist parties: China, Vietnam, Cuba, Laos, North Korea. China, Vietnam and Laos use markets with Party control; Cuba and North Korea keep a command economy. Performance and nationalism, more than Marxism, legitimise rule. All score low on political freedoms. Debate: communism, state capitalism or Leninist developmentalism. Debate questions Can a Leninist party survive indefinitely with a market economy? Which is the more accurate label for China: socialism or capitalism?
Is Marx Still Relevant? Inequality, Platforms and Crisis
The last question

Marx died in 1883 and the states claiming his name have mostly failed or changed. Yet each crisis, from 2008 to the pandemic to AI, brings him back. The question is not whether Marx was right about communism but which of his diagnoses still work.
The return of Marx

After 1989 many pronounced Marxism dead. The 2008 financial crisis revived interest: sales of Capital rose, and Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2013) became a bestseller. In 2018, Marx's 200th birthday drew new attention; Time and The Economist ran cover pieces. Surveys show young people in rich countries are warmer to "socialism" than older generations.
Inequality and concentration

Marx expected capital to concentrate. Today, the top 1% own about 20-30% of income in many countries and a higher share of wealth; the top 1% held about 45% of global wealth by some estimates (UBS, Oxfam). Piketty's law, r > g (capital returns exceed growth), shows wealth accumulating faster than output. The Oxfam 2024 report says the five richest men doubled wealth since 2020. India's top 1% income share is about 22% (World Inequality Lab, 2022-23), among the highest in the world.
Platforms, data and "technofeudalism"

Digital platforms (Amazon, Google, Meta, Uber) concentrate control of markets and data. Some see a new stage: Nick Srnicek ( Platform Capitalism , 2016); Shoshana Zuboff ( Surveillance Capitalism , 2019); Yanis Varoufakis ( Technofeudalism , 2023) arguing capital has become rent. Gig work revives piece-rate and weak job security: delivery workers lack protections, and AI raises the question of automation and unemployment, which Marx touched in the "Fragment on Machines" ( Grundrisse ).
Crisis, climate and global value chains

Capitalism has repeated booms and busts (1929, 1973, 2008), and uses debt and finance. Marxist ideas inform analyses of global value chains, offshoring, and imperialism (Patnaik; Smith, Imperialism in the Twenty-First Century , 2016). The ecological crisis (see 5-0-5) and social reproduction (5-0-4) extend the frame. Political movements range from Bernie Sanders's "democratic socialism" to Mamdani's November 2025 win in New York (he took office on 1 January 2026) (Zohran Mamdani, self-described democratic socialist, elected mayor in November 2025; verify details).
What Marx got wrong

Capitalism did not collapse; real wages rose in rich countries; the middle class grew rather than shrank; the working class split and shrank in industrial countries; revolutions occurred in peasant countries and produced authoritarian states; and the labour theory of value has been abandoned by most economists. Workers' politics shifted toward identity and nationalism. Welfare states, unions and regulation tamed capitalism in the 20th century.
Verdicts

Liberals (Fukuyama, Deirdre McCloskey): capitalism has raised living standards enormously (global extreme poverty fell from about 36% in 1990 to about 9% in 2019, World Bank), and Marx underestimated innovation and adaptation. Economists : Piketty's data is disputed (Auten and Splinter, 2024, find smaller US top-income shares), and inequality between countries fell while within-country inequality rose. Marxists reply that rising rents, monopolies and care crises vindicate him. Anarchists and greens : Marx too statist and productivist. Pragmatists : use Marx as a method, not a doctrine.
Marx and contemporary India

India combines high growth with high inequality, a large informal sector (about 80-90% of workers), contractualisation, farmer protests (2020-21) and the new labour codes (passed 2019-20, with implementation news in 2025). Marxists study agrarian distress (Patnaik), the "jobless growth" debate, and caste-class intersections (Ambedkar, Anand Teltumbde). Kerala's remittance economy and Left Front history provide cases. The BJP and Congress both use the language of welfare; the Left's electoral decline sits alongside intellectual presence in universities and unions.
Five takeaways and two debates

Key takeaways Marx's core diagnoses of concentration, crisis and alienation still frame debates. Piketty and data on inequality revived his themes. Platforms, gig work and AI raise new questions about labour and rent. Failures: no collapse, rising wages, authoritarian revolutions, labour theory abandoned. Marx is useful as a method of critique, less as a blueprint. Debate questions Which Marxian idea survives best: class, crisis, alienation or exploitation? Would a society built on his ideas need more or less state?
